utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May we call the case, please, and at the same time ask the usher already to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just one very brief question because it has to be answered during the next break, we would have the possibility to change from afternoon to morning the 24th of March and the 7th of April. In the past, it was not agreed, but there was strong opinion that it would be better if possible to sit in the morning. Any objections to this rescheduling?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, if we can be advised what is on the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are still in the phase, as you can see from our calendar, rebuttal/rejoinder. And then it will be followed by the closing arguments. But at this point in time, we can't say yet what about the last remaining witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll sit the 24th and the 7th of April in the morning. Then let us continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Trifkovic immediately, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we start, Your Honour, I have some documents that you asked me to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this bundle here, first we have a copy of the first report on voluntary contributions by states from August 1994, which indicates that Malaysia contributed 2 million, and Pakistan 1 million dollars, for a total of 94 point some per cent of 3.2 million that had been contributed. The second item is an article by Alfred Rubin, the distinguished professor of international law that I mentioned yesterday whose article was the basis for my comments in my 1996 article. And the third article is the actual copy of the 1996 article as printed in chronicles, and that's the only one I can really usefully comment upon. Because the website article, as I indicated yesterday, is an added amalgam of two articles which I didn't add it myself. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it first be shown to the Defence first, and then to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the same bundle, yes. They are all the same. In addition, if I'm allowed to offer another one-sheet document, it is a sample of US commentary on my work on Islam. I'm deeply concerned about some of the comments that were made yesterday about my writings on the subject. And I hope that this will simply offer supplementary evidence that at least on the other side of the Atlantic ocean, my writing is considered neither extreme, nor eccentric, nor belonging to the political or ideological margins. It includes the National Review, which is one of the most prominent political magazines in the United States; Investor's Business Daily, which is the second most prominent business newspaper; Jewish World Review; Conservative Book Club; Book List, which is the biggest library trade magazine. I think overall, on a general note, we are witnessing the beginnings of a kind of cognitive -- of the difference between the discourse in the United States and Europe on crucial issues concerning the future of our common civilisation that is not for us to comment today. But for what it's worth, I like to offer this comment as an illustration of where we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this Tribunal, it could only be offered by one of the parties. And therefore, in the moment, nothing has to be said until we have the request by one of the parties that the document be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's of course for Your Honours to draw your conclusions as to what you think of Dr. Trifkovic's work. But I have no objection if he wants to put in what he says the United States thinks of his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't lose any minute in this case. It's a case, again, on the individual responsibility of Dr. Stakic, and this has nothing to do with the United States. There is nothing like "the United States." There are opinions here and there, also on the other side, the fundamental point made yesterday is the clear lack of tolerance, the poor basis of facts relying on secondary instead of primary sources. And not going into details, we discussed some examples yesterday. This is clear. But as I said yesterday, this has nothing to do with Dr. Stakic being the accused here in this Tribunal. And it was making me absolutely hesitant from the beginning of this case to go too much into details of so-called history, because everybody has, no doubt, his own view on history. And this is the good right of everybody. But we have to concentrate on the case against Dr. Stakic, and no inference should be drawn by those articles we were confronted with yesterday. So, please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm going to do is look at what we have been handed over the break and maybe come back to it after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, what happened to the second article, the one that you did write in March 2000?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't find it on the website. It was also published in a magazine, but it wasn't published on the website. What we have in the early 2000 is the amalgam of two published articles which was concocted. Basically, I will be happy to supply it subsequent to my testimony. But that one dealt primarily with the Kosovo situation. I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I know that you managed to get this from the actual issue of chronicles itself, the original 1996 article. Why weren't you able to get the 2000 article?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a total one hour and 45 minutes use of Internet time courtesy of the lady who's -- Isabel. And during that time, I did searches of all of my articles that I could get hold of, and that one, the 1996 article, was available from a third source. The 2000 article was not. Not all articles published in chronicles are posted on the website.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go back, before I continue with your report, to two matters that you dealt with yesterday. At page 3, this was your evidence in chief. When you were asked about Dr. Stakic by Mr. Lukic, you were asked to describe Dr. Stakic's role at page 2 of the LiveNote. And then you said at page 3: "In the period after the spring of 1992, I think particularly poignant is the interview, or rather sorry, the report that we had on the occasion of the bishop's visit to Prijedor." Now, this was a document that was provided by the Defence. And I want to ask you whether it's the one that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was Document 87 in the bundle that the Defence provided to us. I'll give you the original. And if Your Honours can't find it, I'll have the English put up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You are making reference to line 18 through 20 of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It starts at 17 on my copy, Your Honour, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the article dated the 9th of October, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Interethnic relations should be nurtured on mutual trust." Now, the first thing, it's hardly spring of 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I used the term "in the aftermath of the events of spring 1992."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In the period after the spring of 1992," so I mean it didn't occur to you to say autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used the spring of 1992 as the cutoff point which is the dramatic rupture of the city of Prijedor, if you will, and that even in the aftermath of those events, the public discourse of Dr. Stakic continued to contain appeals for mutual trust and reconciliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You told us also yesterday, and this was at page 22, Your Honours, of the LiveNote, that you'd explained to Mr. Ostojic that you don't have much interest, to use the colloquial term, of the "nitty-gritty of who did what to whom" in the municipality of Prijedor. Do I take it from that that you have never looked at the actual detail or at all of what actually happened in Prijedor between May and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the "nitty-gritty" referred specifically to the question which I believe was asked about whether I had looked at the minutes of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly sessions in the period leading up to the spring of 1992. And even though the colloquial term "nitty-gritty" may have been more judiciously chosen, under the circumstances, it specifically referred to the question whether I had actually looked at the verbatim minutes of those meetings of whose existence I wasn't even aware, but I was aware in the course of your question yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you are aware, are you, of the massive scale of - and I use the term in its wide as possible sense - ethnic cleansing that took place in Prijedor during that period?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the massive dislocations of population during that period, and I assure you that the term "nitty-gritty" referred to the minutes of the assembly meetings prior to those events and not to the events themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And so you're aware, are you, of as you put it the dislocation, which involved incarcerating something in the region of 3.000 people in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the incarceration of close to 3.000 people in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware of the attacks that took place on the various villages?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brief was specifically to leave the political and historical analysis of the events at the point where military events pick up, and I was not under the impression that I was to comment in detail on those unless they, of course, pertained to the broader global picture. But in this particular instance, all I can say is that I'm also aware that the actual initial shots in the Municipality of Prijedor were fired at Hambarine and that they were the result of a confrontation between a Muslim barrier and a Yugoslav army convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do I take it that that in your view is justification for the shelling of Kozarac and Hambarine which took place after that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that a military expert will be better qualified to answer what is appropriate response to that kind of provocation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You see, your report is actually headed "The Events in Prijedor, 1991 to 1992." Didn't you think, if you were going to produce a report on the events in Prijedor, that you ought to know what those events were?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not deny that I have a fairly accurate picture of what those events are. It is one thing to have that accurate picture or at least relatively detailed picture; it is another to be asked to comment on what I can only describe as a question appropriate for the military expert to answer, like what is the appropriate military response to the confrontation at Hambarine checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for an opinion as a military expert. I'm asking you for an opinion as a human being who says he knows what happened.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a human being, I believe that it is very important to consider the effect of the initial shots being fired in an electrified situation. It is tantamount to screaming "fire" in a crowded movie theatre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you didn't read the minutes either of the SDS club or the assembly because you felt that that didn't tell you more than, for example, the articles.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also that I was operating under certain time restraints, that had I been given the brief that would entail a greater number of hours that could be devoted to this issue, I assure you that I would have been able to devote myself both to these primary sources and to the production of a more detailed and better footnoted report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Equally, I think -- sorry, I have been warned already about question and answer. Equally, I think you told us that to some extent, it was your opinion that the speeches and the things that were being said were with an eye to the future as it were.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the point that I made in reference to frankly all three ethnic sides in the Bosnian dispute, that from the early fall of 1991, on all sides, there is a great deal of posturing where ostensible reasons for actions and statements are on one side, and substantive hidden agenda on the other. And this is not the monopoly of any one side in these proceedings, and that's why I wanted to imply that there is sometimes less than meets the eye in the primary documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you this: Did it ever occur to you, when you looked at this article, that by the time Dr. Stakic and Bishop Komarica were meeting, that there were almost [Realtime transcript read in error "also"] no Muslims to worry about in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one thing to emphasise the facts of the changed ethnic picture at the period under consideration in this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Ms. Korner is testifying, that's okay. But if she asked a question, she should present to the witness the documentation on which she is basing her statement "no Muslims in Prijedor area at that time." That's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said actually "almost." I see it says "also," but I actually said "almost." Look, if Mr. Ostojic wants to make the objection, he can make the objection. Two people doing it is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the demographer of the Prosecution who testified here, this statement is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we can agree on a limited number from both sides. Okay. Please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The changed ethnic picture in Prijedor at the time under consideration does not alter the fact that in his public pronouncements, Dr. Stakic continued to appeal on ethnic reconciliation. This is something that I think was the primary focus of your initial question. And my reply is that if, regardless of the circumstances, there is one constant in these unfortunate times from the fall of 1991 to the fall of 1992, it is Stakic's continued insistence on ethnic reconciliation and the mitigable absence of what could colloquially be termed "hate speech" in his discourse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you that Dr. Stakic was making these statements for public consumption?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Dr. Stakic was merely making these statements for public consumption, then he is both notably disingenuous, because that means that he had been making similar statements merely for public consumption even at the time when other members of nationalist parties, Serbs included, were making far less tolerant statements. And I'm talking about the fall of 1991 and the winter of 1991/1992. On the basis of the continuity of those statements from the period when he was under no compulsion to make statements for public consumption only, I believe that these statements reflected his inner most convictions rather than public posturing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know Dr. Stakic from Adam. You've met him twice for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I insist is that if we look at the continuity of public statements, as reflected in the published sources such as Kozarski Vjesnik, they point out Dr. Stakic as a notably conciliatory person as compared to other people in the SDA, HDZ, or SDS establishments of the period. I'm simply making this statement regardless of whether I know him or not. Even without ever meeting Dr. Stakic, I would have stated the same because I looked at six or seven different statements spread from November and December of 1991, and January and February of 1992, on to October of 1992. Very different to what was coming out from less responsible members of the political leaderships of the other two parties or even Dr. Stakic's own party in some instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I just want one final question on this topic: Is it your -- is it not your experience that public figures have said something in public and done quite the opposite?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is almost invariably the case with seasoned professional politicians. It is, however, my impression on the basis both of documentation and the brief personal encounter on two different occasions that far from being a seasoned and cunning politician, Dr. Stakic was an eminent political novice quite possibly out of his depth in the whirlwind of circumstances beyond his control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your impression, is it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back, please, now to your report, then. We left off yesterday at page 8. I was asking you about the numbers of Bosnian Muslims in German uniform. You footnoted at footnote 13 "Professor Donia's willingness to cite without comment a Partisan claim," et cetera. That's your comment, is it, on what was in his report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my comment which I don't think is crucial to the main body of the report but which is nevertheless worthy of passing note which is why it is in the footnote and not in the main body of the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only question I want to ask you about that is you say: "It is typical of how foreign observers of the Bosnian scene have often been willing to take as fact what they wanted to hear." Is it your opinion that the only people who are able to comment on the Bosnian scene are people who come from there or come from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what I meant to say is that when it comes to the period of World War II, in particular, outsiders have been prone to accept what one could only term "parallel myths" on different sides at something approaching face value. In the case of Great Britain, one could mention the proponents of the partisan myth such as the late Professor William Deakin and the late brigadier Fitzroy McLean or the exponents of the Mihailovich myth such as the late Captain Michael Lees. I mention them simply because there is a tendency to look at the romanticised, beautified narrative of one or the other parties in these proceedings and achieve personal identification with them that goes beyond the critical faculties of a strictly detached academic observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: See, you don't qualify this at all. You say how foreign observers, full stop. Are you actually saying all foreign observers or some?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, some, definitely some. It would be absurd to say all because we have excellent foreign observers who have been able to look beyond the smokescreen of parallel historiographies with axes to grind. But in this particular case, simply to claim that many, is the term used, I believe, is very vague and not helpful, and not accurately descriptive of the situation on the ground in 1941.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I really don't want to spend too long on this. But you don't say "many," you make an assertion that foreign observers. If you look at your footnote page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, when I say "foreign observers of the Bosnian scene," I specifically meant a number of academics who have taken sides vis-a-vis the civil war in Yugoslavia and with particular reference to the war in Bosnia. I mentioned some of them in the British context. I could go on. I don't think it's of particular importance to the report itself. Suffice to say that for about 50 years after the end of World War II, in Yugoslavia there had been something of an internus [phoen] in warfare going on in the Western academia on the subjects of Tito, Mihailovich, the Allied policy, the aborted landing in the Balkans, Churchill's peripheral strategy versus Eisenhower's direct strategy and so on. This is a long subject, and I use something as a shorthand in my footnote without for a moment implying that it meant all, but it means a considerable number of academics who without necessarily having flawed personal motives, wholeheartedly identify with a given narrative in the Yugoslav civil war saga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I say I don't want to spend too much time. This next page, please, page 9, a further footnote there criticising Robert -- Professor Donia who you assert is not a Second World War historian. Would you describe your second as a Second World War historian?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would describe myself as a historian and political scientist who has taken particular interest in Second World War. My Ph.D. was on the subject of World War II, and my post doctoral research at Hoover institution was also on the subjects of World War II and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on to allege, "has accepted of the Titoist myth-making at face value. His suggestion, Prijedor report op.cit. p. 3, that 'each side suffered thousands of casualties...' is wrong and misleading." Do you have Dr. Donia's report there?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if you could be given a copy by the Defence. They must have it I take it. It's also an exhibit, I'm told. Dr. Donia's report on Prijedor. Now, can you look, please, at page 3 where Dr. Donia says that each side suffered casualties. I'm told it's SK42. Thank you very much. You'll see it's in the second paragraph, after the footnote 6: "The badly outnumbered partisans fought valiantly, and each side suffered thousands of casualties in the battle for control of Mount Kozara." And he footnotes his source for that as Mr. Enver Redic. Have you read that book?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. What I have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait, just a moment. I'll come on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying you haven't read that book.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then go on to say in your footnote: "The Germans took some casualties (several dozen), and the Partisans suffered hundreds of dead, but not thousands. The thousands that perished were Serb civilians." What is your source for asserting that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As far as the German casualties are concerned, there is the war diary of the -- German high command. It's the widely available source, the original is in the [German spoken] militare archive. And it is under signature OKWKTB. The several dozen is correct. The several thousand does not apply even if you include the Ustasha casualties and the Domobran casualties, even if you factor them in addition to the Germans, you're looking at hundreds not thousands. In the same way, if you look at the Zvornik Dokumenata, which is the standard source, primary source collection for partisan historiography of World War II which is in Serbo-Croat called Zvornik Dokumenata O Narodnooslobodilackom. The annals of documents on people's liberation struggle, they have also fairly detailed evidence of the losses of individual partisan units in the Kozara region. And also, they have not so detailed, rather rough, estimates of the number of Serbian civilians from Kozara foothold villages who were deported in the aftermath of the collapse of partisan resistance in the area, and that number goes, of course, into the many thousands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We were never allowed to interrupt the answer of any answer of any of the Prosecution witnesses. So please let the witness finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm merely trying to move this along. But I'm quite happy, if the witness wants to say something more, he may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What I'm trying to emphasise is my comments in this footnote reflect factual state of affairs. Why didn't I elaborate any further? Well, because I didn't believe that it was particularly important to this report. I wanted to keep the historical review reasonably succinct, but nevertheless give the proper historical context. The plain facts of the case are as follows: The German regular army suffered relatively minor casualties in the Kozara operation in 1942. It was by the way, again, this is part and parcel of the partisan myths, a regular occurrence all over the former Yugoslavia. In Serbia proper, for instance, it was for the killing of 26 regular German soldiers that thousands of hostages were shot at Kraguljevic. The partisan resistance was very effective in causing counter measures which served Tito's purpose of having as many recruits into his ranks as possible. But the Partizan resistance certainly until 1943 was not very effective in inflicting large casualties on the regular German army. In the clashes between partisans and German regulars, it was the Germans who had the upper hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've finished. Doctor, why didn't you footnote your sources for the assertions?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been a footnote within a footnote. I believe that the claim that I'm making here is so well known to the professionals that it was almost superfluous. As far as the losses of respective sides in World War II are concerned, at least for as efficient a bureaucratic administrative command and control machinery as the Weimarch, there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do understand the reason, don't you, as a historian, for footnoting the source for the assertions that you make, so that people can check it.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is possible to check the source of Dr. Donia's; it is not possible to check a single word of what you've said today without considerable research.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is unfortunate that in particular, the footnote that Dr. Donia provided for the claim about thousands of casualties was worse than no footnote at all because it referred to a work that I have not seen, but that plainly contains inaccuracies because if his footnote is sourced to that particular book that you mention, and it claims that each side suffers thousands of casualties, which is patently not true, then it's really preferable to stick to what I would call well-known facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you really want to say that a book you've never looked at, never read, have no idea what the author is, must be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the book claims that there were thousands of casualties inflicted on both sides of the German partisan divide in 1942 in the Kozara battle, I claim without looking at the book that it is totally inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, please, at the next page, page 10, where we have another footnote correcting Professor Donia's innocent recapitulation of partisan myths, et cetera. You say: "The Serbs in the area of Prijedor far from having a master plan and strategy were confused and worried." On what do you base that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I base that on is the obvious lack of self-confidently triumphant tone in different articles and editorials from the Kozarski Vjesnik. And since I do not know people from Prijedor personally, I haven't been to the area, this is the only source that I can go by. Some of them are definitely nostalgic for the old order. The Vjesnik in the fall of 1991 is full of articles invoking the socialist legacy and full of pronouncements by the veterans' association or by the movement for Yugoslavia. At other times, you will have readers' letters rhapsodising nostalgic about the period of ethnic harmony, peace, and tolerance. And at the same time nervous voices expressing alarm at the violence going on next door in Croatia, expressing concern about the plummeting living standards and the collapse of municipal services that were supposed to be provided by the commune. There is no sense, and I am now not referring to any particular article per se, there is no sense of a vibrantly self-confident, strong and assertive community on the march to its clearly defined objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you never read any of the documents that the Serbs themselves produced during and before the relevant time, how can you assert that this wasn't planned and organised?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we are talking about the documents that the Serbian democratic party, the SDS, produced, we are talking about one segment of the Serbian opinion in Prijedor. In the footnote under consideration and in response to your question, we are talking about the Serbs collectively. And I will submit to you that the Serbian democratic party in Prijedor was not the sole expression of the Serb opinion, that certainly the Serbs as a collective did not have a united voice in what they want; if anything, they had a -- just about the only thing they had in common was what they did not want, which was to be taken out of Yugoslavia against their will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move, please, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just, that we need not come back to this. What is the source for you coming to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, which particular conclusion, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The last conclusion you made, that -- "I submit to you that the Serbian democratic party in Prijedor was not the sole expression of the Serb opinion, that certainly the Serbs as a collective did not have a united voice in what they want." How can you come to this collation, based on what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated earlier, based on the cross section of articles that were not directly political in the Kozarski Vjesnik which deal with issues such as the conditions in the municipality, the state of education, the state of supplies, the problem of the influx of refugees from Bosnia, the dislocation of families, the problems caused by the absence of reservists belonging to the two units from Prijedor sent to Slavonia in the summer and fall of 1991, all of which -- and again, if I were to expand on this, if I had time, it could be an interesting exercise in social anthropology. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just asked about the source and I take it from your answer that your mere and sole source was Kozarski Vjesnik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- A well-disputed and contested newspaper even by witnesses of the Defence, telling us that this to a certain extent and on concrete examples is not a reliable source. And you, as an expert, as you sit here, believe that's enough for an expert testimony - and I put the same question of course to Mr. Donia as well - to rely on these secondary sources instead of going into details of the archives? I understood that you have never been in Prijedor, that you never tried to go to archives in Prijedor or Banja Luka, that you never tried to get access to other sources, being not only minutes, but reports on the meetings of the Serbian Assembly, of the Municipal Assembly, of Crisis Staff, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, my question: Is it in fact true you relied on these articles and merely you received from the Defence, or did you try to investigate yourself on the basis of other articles, other newspapers available at the time in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I preceded my statement about my impression about the overall state of affairs, and I'm talking about nonpolitical aspects of the life in Prijedor. I preceded it by saying that it was based on my comprehensive reading of the collection of this newspaper which I believe in the period of late 1991 was not necessarily unreliable because it was under multiethnic management and editorial control. Also, I believe that I emphasised, again in the preamble to my previous statement, that it is within the inherent limitations of that sourcing that I'm making this assessment. And that assessment concerns the mood of the people as a whole and not of the political class, not of the political activists and political decision-makers in the municipality. The question from the Prosecution concerned my statement in the footnote, that the Serbs, far from having a master plan and strategy, were confused and worried. If you want to get the impression of self-confident and vibrant and strident community that knows which way it's heading, and that it has firm marching orders to clearly defined objectives, I'm afraid you certainly will not find it in this source as an illustration of the Serbian collective frame of mind in Prijedor in late 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to page 13. Sorry. Can we go to page 13, please, of your report. In the third paragraph, you say: "Even without the vividly remembered trauma of the Second World War, they reacted in 1991-1992 just as the Anglophone citizens of Texas or Arizona might do if they are outvoted, one day, in a referendum demanding those states' incorporation into Mexico." How did you come by that analogy?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analogy is clearly aimed at implying that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. I'm sorry to interrupt. But we may get on quicker. I'm just asking how you came by that analogy, Texas or Arizona. I understand you come from Chicago.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Texas and Arizona happen to be the states in which the Latino plurality is likely to turn into majority before the end of this decade. Of course, most Latinos are enthusiastic to be Americans. They move north across the Rio Grande to get away from Mexico, not to move Mexico with them. So the illustration had purely the purpose of making a parallel that doesn't have necessarily immediate political relevance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is this an original thought by you? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point has been made that the shifting balance in the far southwest of the United States may cause some Latino activists to demand what they are calling la Republica Del Norte or to redeem the lands lost in the Mexican war of 1848/9. But -- so I don't think the notion is altogether original, but it is something that could have its equivalence in other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it taken directly from an article in chronicles by somebody called David Hartman, who I believe is head of your Rockford Institute?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, the notion is not original. I'm not aware of David Hartman having used it, but it is something that has been considered by a number of analysts what will happen if the shifting population change in the far southwest results in demands for constitutional changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hartman, do you remember Mr. Hartman writing an article called "Reflection on a Texan's Visit to Mexico"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to have a look at the excerpt?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking why you don't give him credit for this --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I assure you that the parallel between the issue of self-determination and the shifting ethnic balance in a locality concerning border lands of the United States is neither original nor remarkable, that it is something that if we were to do a Google search, I'm sure we could come up with dozens of authors discussing similar issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you turn, please, to page 16. You say there, again, this time it's criticism of Noel Malcolm, it's your footnote 27 where I think you're dealing with -- yes, you're dealing with the Izetbegovic declaration. And you state there that: "he accepts the 'achievements" -- this is at the top of page 16 -- "of Euro-American civilisation' but only in the area of science and technology... we shall have to accept them if we wish to survive." And you criticise there Noel Malcolm for failing to mention that Izetbegovic specifically defined the acceptable achievements of western civilisation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like, please, to it -- forgive me for one moment. I just want to find... I just want to jump ahead for a moment, please, to page 27. You quote a book by Messrs. Burg and Shoup, I think it's pronounced. Shoup, Shoup. Right, your footnote 62, and then 63, where you assert that: The HDZ ostensible support for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina was but so much lip service, however, because in the same month the HDZ set up a 'Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna' in western Herzegovina and central Bosnia, as well as a 'Croatian Community of the Bosnian Sava Valley.'" And that comes from them, does it? You're giving your source there.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the way, when it comes to the activities of the HDZ, both in western Herzegovina and Central Bosnia and in the Sava River valley, we have again a plethora of documents from Croatian sources which have been made available to me subsequent to the preparation of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to have a look, please, at page 47 and 48 of their book and tell me where you see that particular phrase that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, "One cannot help but be struck by the hard and crude documents produced in the course of the debate. Documents that address the most delicate of all questions in Bosnian politics in a highly provocative language," page 79.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, no, no. 47 and 48, please. I'm so sorry. I misled you. It's marked you will see. You have got a quote under 62, 79, and then for 63, ibid, 47 to 48, which it refers to, as I understand it, "the same month the HDZ set up a 'Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna' in western Herzegovina and Central Bosnia as well as a 'Croatian Community of the Bosnian Sava Valley.'"

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second. This was a mistake for which I apologise. It was Kumar's, ibid, because of the vagaries of my word processing system in the editing remained as ibid which ostensibly relates to Burg and Shoup. In fact, it relates to Kumar's book which is referenced on the previous page as footnote 58, page 49; footnote 61 should be referenced Kumar, pages 47 to 48. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, can we go back to, please, page -- the one we're looking at, which was page -- I've forgotten the page now. 16.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me something, Dr. Trifkovic: Do you know somebody called Professor Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of Nenad Kecmanovic. I have not met him in person, or if I have, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ever read anything he's written?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read a number of his articles in the form of personal reminiscences in the Knin weekly, the Belgrade weekly, in the period after his transfer from Sarajevo to Belgrade in the mid-1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to have a look, please, at a report written by him. Have you ever seen that report before?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this report was put in for the purposes, I think, and I'm now pretty sure but I'll check that, for the Bosanski Samac case, Simic and others. And Ms. Sutherland who can recognise an indictment number just like that assures me that is in fact the Simic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, to turn to page 6 of that report. Could you read, please, paragraph 10 of that report.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In a revealing sentence, Izetbegovic discusses the status of non-Muslims in countries with Muslim majority: 'The non-Muslims minorities within an Islamic state, on condition that are they are loyal, enjoy religious freedom and all protection.' However as" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause. That's all I need. Thank you. Now, can you look, please, at the middle of the paragraph of the top paragraph, page 16, after the footnote 27.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. "In a revealing sentences Izetbegovic discusses the status of non-Muslims in countries with Muslim majorities: 'The non-Muslim minorities within an Islamic state, on condition that they are loyal, emphasis added, enjoyed religious freedom and all protection.'"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's actually identical word for word, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except that the quote is mine because it comes from my own article on Izetbegovic's Islamic declaration that was published -- I don't know what is the date of this report. But I will be happy to furnish the reference to the particular --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he has copied from your article without giving you any credit for that? In the words -- word for word, "in a revealing sentence..."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not at liberty to comment whether he has done so or not. What I can assure you most emphatically is that this particular formation in my report is mine and mine alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, you told us that the footnote, in a typical distortion, footnote number 27, "In a typical distortion, Noel Malcolm writes in this connection..." Et cetera, et cetera. Now, look at Professor Kecmanovic's, footnote 11.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that he copied that from you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, look at what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look first of all, your footnote 27 which you said was your comment on Noel Malcolm. "In a typical distortion, Noel Malcolm writes in this connection..." and so on and so forth. Now have a look at the footnote 11 on Dr. Kecmanovic's report at page 6.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as it happens, the comment on the typical distortion of Noel Malcolm is neither Kecmanovic's nor mine. The notion of typical distortion comes from a comment that was made, and I am now quoting from memory, at a conference on Noel Malcolm's book "Bosnia, Short History" by Jovan Zametica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Trifkovic. I understood and I asked you this quite carefully that these comments, these footnotes, were your comments. Are you now saying they are neither yours nor Professor Kecmanovic's, but somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The notion of typical distortion in particular. But what I would add is my article on the Izetbegovic Islamic declaration is available, and it clearly antedates whatever may be the date of this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This report is dated December 2002. Your report, as I understand it, was handed in in February of this year.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you that my article dealing with Izetbegovic's Islamic declaration antedates 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll ask you one last time. How is it that both of you in identical words refer to Mr. Noel Malcolm's book?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the particular footnote that both of us use, we have referred obviously to the same source, which is the proceeds of a conference on Noel Malcolm's book held at the Serbian Academy of Science in Belgrade in, I believe, late 1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So quite by chance, both of you picked on that --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pure coincidence, that's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so because I assure you, one, that I have never seen this report and, two, that I would not knowingly copy from this, but at the same time the formulation offered in that particular round table discussion was very felicitous and obviously appealing to both of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, shall we. Okay, could we move to page 19 in your report, please. Do you see in the middle of the first paragraph the sentence beginning: "Inevitably, these events were bound to have profound consequences on Bosnia and Herzegovina, which 'had survived, despite its history of ethnic violence and social conflict'..." et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you cite for that Burg and Shoup again.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at the bottom of page 8 of Professor Kecmanovic's report. And in paragraph 15, do you see the sentence beginning: "Inevitably, what was happening in the rest of Yugoslavia was bound to have profound consequences on Bosnia and Herzegovina which was often described as Yugoslavia in miniature." Do you agree almost identical, the odd word changed here and there, to what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask one more time, what exactly is the date of the Kecmanovic report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date of the Kecmanovic report is I believe, and I'll check that, September -- sorry, this is in fact the report -- I should add the report was actually written in Serbo-Croat, and the translation, if we look at page 60, was on the 19th of September 2002.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Ostojic to confirm that the draft of my report, which contained this very formulation, was handed -- when does he to the best of his recollection remember my giving it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic can't testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back and look at what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me while I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because I asked you this at the beginning of cross-examination yesterday. Right. What you said yesterday was that, at page 23 of the LiveNote: "I prepared the first draft of the report shortly after Christmas. In fact, in the first week of the new year." And then I asked you how long had it taken you. And then you said: "My report was completed in the second week of February."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what I meant to say is the first draft which wasn't the report itself, and this is something that I will obviously have to get to the bottom of. Having circulated the salient points that I intended to include in the report via the Internet with a number of my contacts around. I don't know Dr. Kecmanovic, but without wanting to implicate anyone in willful plagiarism, all I can say is that this language is mine, not his. What I have done is in the preparation of the report was to send Internet messages to a number of colleagues, inviting their commentary and opinion on certain points that I wanted to raise in my reports. Some of them seem to have been passed on without my authorisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to understand what you're telling us. You are asserting that Professor Kecmanovic, whose full report was translated in September 2002, so we can take it that he must have written it sometime before that in Serbo-Croat --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me finish -- has somehow or other acquired your exact language - and believe you me, Mr. Trifkovic, we're going to come to a lot more fuller similarities later on - but somehow or other, he has plagiarised a report that you hadn't written. Is that what you're really telling --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is it is common and established practice among academics in certain fields to circulate drafts of their papers and to circulate ideas for either reports or scientific submissions and invite comments. What I'm telling you now is that I had no access to this report at the time of writing my own report, and I had no knowledge of its existence. I do not know if and when it was actually made available either on the Internet or in hard copy or circulated to members of the public. Could you elucidate me on that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't help you often that, at least not at the moment. But I just want to read to you what you said about this yesterday, Dr. Trifkovic. I asked you -- I apologise to the interpreters. I know I'm jumping in. "Dr. Trifkovic, when were you instructed to first prepare this report?" Page 21 of the LiveNote. At first you said: "I was not instructed to prepare it. I was approached by Mr. Ostojic who I had known personally for some years, with a view to my potential role as an expert witness for the Defence. After a number of rather sporadic meetings at several weeks' distance, being the period of September, October, I think that we clarified the shape and the terms of the report sometime in November of last year 2002." Now, are you saying now that you had been circulating on the Internet by September, before you had clarified the shape of the report with Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the language that you were going to use?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was circulating it later. What, however, is apparent is that many formulations which, by the way, are often contained in different writings, specifically we referred earlier to Izetbegovic's Islamic declaration, is not necessarily original writing in that particular instance prepared purpose-written for the report but picked up from different previously published or unpublished materials. What I am particularly insistent is that the reference to the Burg and Shoup has already been contained in my papers presented elsewhere. I do not want to comment on the second quote that you have just given because I would need to verify that. I once again want to emphasise that I have never seen this report, and once again ask when was it made public. When was it circulated?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the answer. I mean, I don't suppose to answer your questions, Dr. Trifkovic. But I have no idea whether it was made public or what. But that's not the point, is it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the point, because if you're implying that I had access to this report and was making use of Professor Kecmanovic's formulations in the preparation of mine, then the obvious implication is that I had access to the report which I now claim and assert under oath that I did not. And therefore it is a perfectly legitimate question for me to ask is when and how was it made available to the members of the public?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or unless you were given it by somebody.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I submit to you that this wasn't the case, that I do not have access to this report and this is the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go through it. I want you to look, now, please, your paragraph, page 19. Second paragraph: "In the Bosnian context an early omen was the non-Serbs parties' refusal to constitute the Council for Questions of Equality of Nations, the projected constitutional linchpin of the multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1990 Amendment 70 of the Republic's Constitution provided for the formation of this body of sixty deputies, twenty each from the three constituent nations, which would decide - strictly by consensus - on all questions referred to it by at least twenty deputies in the lower house of the Assembly..." and so on. You've no footnote for this. Where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the amendment 70 of the constitution is a matter of public record. And I was not under the impression that it's necessary to footnote public documents are generally accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Did you look at it before you wrote this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at the amendments to the 1990 constitution some years ago. I had notes about the amendment 70 in particular, which was by the way a matter of great debate and disputation at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer to the question is no you didn't look at.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look at it specifically in preparation of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you have a look, please, at a copy of the Official Gazette of the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We'll give you the B/C/S. And therefore, Dr. Stakic has a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One question for the Prosecution that we don't lose the order: Do you want to tender the two pages of the book you referenced to earlier this morning? Is it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think it's necessary. He said it's not there. It's an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then you want to tender the report by Professor Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That would be then S414A. And I take it that it's available in B/C/S also for Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll check that, Your Honour. I imagine it must have been for the purposes of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because it was written in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So provisionally marked as 414. And the Official Gazette as of 31 July 1990 is already 65 terred or even admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think it is, Your Honour. Ms. Karper checked and I don't think we have put this in before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's provisionally mark it as S415A, B respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that it's headed: "Decision on the Proclamation of the Amendments 59 Through to 80 of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Constitution"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please go to item number 10. "A Council for issues of achieving equality among peoples and nationalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall be formed in the SRBiH Assembly. The Council shall comprise an equal number of representatives of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, and the appropriate number of representatives from other peoples, nationalities and groups living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the Council shall make its decisions based on agreement of the members of all the peoples and nationalities." Now go back to what you wrote. Paragraph 19: "Amendment 70...provided for the formation of this body of sixty deputies, twenty each from the three constituent nations..." Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say in the amendment 70 itself, but in the debates concerning the formation of this body in the period after the constitution of the multiparty assembly following the November 1990 election, it was suggested that because this specific number was not mentioned in the amendment, that this would be, indeed, the scope of the body. When I say "suggested," I admit that this wasn't contained in the amendment itself; it was a matter of suggestion from parliamentary floor subsequent to the multiparty election.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's an error? The way you state it is an error, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a formal error insofar as it's referenced to the amendment 70. There was no serious dispute -- there was the dispute over the formation of the body itself. There was no serious dispute that if and when it were to be constituted, it would not be larger than 60 MPs because otherwise it would unwieldly and there is no need for a bigger body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is an error which you could have avoided had you checked by looking at the amendment.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I looked at the amendment itself again, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, at page 14 of Professor Kecmanovic's statement, paragraph 26. And do you see the words: "In 1990, amendment 70 --"

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To the constitution, provided for the formation..." yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Identical words to you with the identical error.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One more time: Since I have circulated some drafts of my elements of this report to different addressees, I would have to check on the origin of -- is this translation done in-house in The Hague, the translation of Dr. Kecmanovic's report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I'm not supposed to answer your questions. But the answer is I believe not. I believe it was done by someone on his behalf. There's a name given. Belgrade, it was done.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I have some clear idea of -- that may explain this, but I would prefer not to state it in open court without checking the facts of the case first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you every opportunity, Dr. Trifkovic, to provide this Court with an explanation as to how two reports, one written in September and one only produced in February, or certainly not before autumn, have identical wording and identical mistakes. Do you want to offer any further explanation before the break?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this stage. What I would like to emphasise is that the vagaries of electronic communication of our time and age allow for all kinds of strange things to happen. If you were able to assure me now that the translation of this report was effected by the in-house translators here at The Hague, I would be totally at a loss to explain what was going on. In view of the fact that some the elements of my writings not directly related to this report have been widely circulated and are around, I would have to explore several things. One, is who is the translator of the Kecmanovic report; two, to what extent was the material I had circulated prior to the submission of the report passed on by the recipients to third-party addressees. It may be a heck of a job, but I assure you that I have every intent of getting to the bottom of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean you've made this mistake about the amendment 70 in your writings before?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I mean to say is that the notes that were used in the preparation of this report have been circulated in different forms and in different contexts over a period of years, not necessarily only since September or October of last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, what difference does it make if it was translated in The Hague or it was translated in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you exactly what difference it does make. It makes a great deal of difference indeed. If it was translated in The Hague, then there is no explanation for the possible cut and paste misuse of third-party material by the person adopting the material or creatively translating it. If on the other hand it was done in Belgrade, then there is every possibility of what one might call creative use - and again this is no comment on Dr. Kecmanovic, more on the translator, and I would greatly appreciate the details of this, because it is obviously a matter of my personal prestige and reputation, and I do not intend to leave it at that. What I may also add is that I have faced problems with student plagiarism in the use of unattributed quotes in essays in the course of my university career, and it is very easy on the basis of the signature that Word for Windows leaves in the creation of documents if one is forensically minded in this respect to establish the sequence of events and the precise steps leading to one or another source of attached documents. And in this case, I am talking about attached Word for Windows documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, maybe you better --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just finish this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're suggesting, Dr. Trifkovic, is this: Dr. Kecmanovic, having plagiarised your articles, whatever was on the Internet, translated from the English into Serbo-Croat, and then had it translated back again into English for the purposes of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. Not at all. What I'm suggesting is that certain segments of this report have been obviously used by both Dr. Kecmanovic and me from the same source that authorised its use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What source would that be?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is something that I would like to check before I disclose in open court, that in this particular case, that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you suggest, Dr. Trifkovic, that you and Professor Kecmanovic obtained what was erroneous information about amendment 70?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Dr. Jovan Zametica of Herceg Novi in Montenegro who acted as my research assistant for the background of the amendment 70 situation in the Bosnian assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in September of 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry. I thought you told us a minute ago, Dr. Trifkovic, that you hadn't checked on the amendment because you looked at your notes.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't checked on the amendment because I relied on the notes that I specifically went to the location in order to enlist the help of this expert - I regard him as a highly qualified expert - who prepared the notes for me on the background of amendment 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a convenient moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask the Prosecution, would it be possible to conclude within the next 90 minutes that we can give the Defence the possibility - I don't know what time is needed from your perspective in the moment - that we really can conclude the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For now, not more than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay, then I invite the parties to do their very best.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it depends. I can conclude if I leave out a lot of the stuff that I intend to ask. But it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try to proceed as soon as possible. I can't say any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, let's just finish off, please, your page 19. You say under lost opportunities for peace: "The three ruling parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina (SDA, SDS, HDZ,) managed in the first half of 1991 to cooperate quite smoothly in the power-sharing exercise." Could you look, please, at page 9 of Professor Kecmanovic's report.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I have tried during the break to reconstruct the exact sequence of events, and it was as follows -- and because of the importance of the issue, I would like to state this on record. I made a specific trip to Montenegro in late September of 1992 in order to consult with Dr. Zametica on some of the issues pertaining to the period in question. It is quite common in the preparation of similar reports to rely on research notes of colleagues in the field. On that occasion, he has supplied me with some of his notes which he specifically assured me had been neither published nor circulated, which is why I made the specific inquiry as to whether this material incorporated in Kecmanovic's report had been circulated elsewhere or translated in-house here at The Hague or in Belgrade. Obviously, had I been aware that the material supplied to me with the assurance that these were background notes I'm free to use as I deem fit, being published, and especially being incorporated in another report that was being presented to this Court, I would not have used them. In fact, I had no great overriding need to use them either, but because I respect Dr. Zametica's experience and judgement in this field, and especially since on that occasion he also supplied me with a number of useful newspaper articles from the period in question, I had no reason to believe that there was indeed an overlap. I am stating this for the record now, and I intend to clarify the matter with him and other parties concerned, that I was given the background notes of the elements of my report that overlap with Dr. Kecmanovic's report from Dr. Jovan Zametica with the assurance that these were unpublished, uncirculated research notes which I am free to use and incorporate as I deem fit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be more than happy to continue comparing the two sets. What I wish to assure you once again most emphatically is that this is the sort of confusion that may only result from the dual use of the same set of notes of which I had not been aware at the time of their presentation to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, where are those notes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are Dr. Zametica's notes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the form of a computer diskette at my home in Chicago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you haven't got them here?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you ever say, for the purposes of this report, that Dr. Zametica had provided the notes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he specifically requested not to be named in the proceedings. He prefers not to advertise his contribution to the proceedings. I don't think he wanted either glory or certainly the arrangement was amicable and not pecuniary in any sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, and I believe before, that you had written this report.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is perfectly common practice in the preparation of reports of academic kind to rely on the assistance of research -- of research aides. And in this context, I don't think that my report contains more than 8 or 10 per cent of his contributions. Those notes were given to me with the assurance that they were in no sense circulated prior or used by anyone else prior to their presentation to me. Otherwise, of course, it would be simply ridiculous to rely on the same set of background notes as someone else had done before. But all I can assure you is that I have a suspicion that both reports relied on the same set of notes. I have no reason to believe that Dr. Zametica had lifted his notes from Dr. Kecmanovic's report and passed them on to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just make this clear. You said September 1992. You mean September 2002?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, September 2002, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're now saying that this Dr. Zametic --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zametica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Must have provided sometime before he gave them to you his notes to Professor Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's the only inference I'm forced to make at this moment because I haven't been able to contact him and explore the facts of the case. I assure you that what I am giving you now is not only the whole truth, but nothing but the truth, that there would have been no earthly reason for me to rely on notes which I had any suspicion had been used, let alone used in this particular institution, especially since, as I emphasise, the practice of relying on background research by either formal or friendly assistants is neither remarkable nor unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "notes"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean are references to certain elements of the developments between the constitution of the multiparty assembly in November of 1990 and the collapse of -- basically the aftermath of the referendum of February 29th/March 1st. When I say "notes," I specifically mean references to constitutional and third-party comments on constitutional developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to understand. You're talking about notes referring no doubt to sources, to constitutional aspects and the like.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not narrative.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The narrative itself in this case, which you mentioned specifically, concerning the 60 deputies, of course, is overlapping, and I assure you it comes from that same source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we could go on forever doing this in the report, but I want to take you then to the most glaring example now, please, straight away. Can you go, please, to page 33 of your report. The section headed "One Last Chance for Peace: The Cuteleiro Plan." The narrative there I take it was written by you whether or not based on notes from Dr. -- whatever his name is.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zametica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is largely based on his background notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based, but did you write this narrative?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to check it against the original file in order to verify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you look now at page 25 of Professor Kecmanovic's report. Paragraph 52 headed in his report: "The Cutileiro Plan." Paragraph 52 is identical in every single word I suggest to paragraph 1 on page 33. Paragraph 53 is identical in every single word to paragraph 2 on page 33. Paragraph 54 is identical word for word to the third paragraph on your page 33. Paragraph 55 identical word for word to the fourth paragraph on page 33. On paragraph 56, if you go to page 27 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 56 in the professor's report, top of page 34 of yours, the only difference is "nevertheless" in Professor Kecmanovic's report, and you simply start, "The agreement seemed promising at first."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
