utterances.text: This whole page is obviously Dr. Zametica's, and I would emphasise that in the context of 40 pages of my report, a total of about three pages that were included from the notes given to me as originals, free for use, without reference and without attributation, is neither original nor remarkable, that it is indeed normal practice in the context of preparation of scientific papers to rely on inputs from associates and collaborators. Had I been made aware of the fact that the same material was shared by others, I would not have used them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would you do with a student when you identify in two similar works such an identical part, page by page, word by word, the same wording? What would be your reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My reaction would be to institute an investigation and find out why did the overlap happen. In this case I am again assuring Your Honour that this was due to my honest -- being honestly misled into the belief that the background notes provided by an associate who volunteered to share this material with me and to use it as I deemed fit was given on the understanding that it was neither circulated nor published, nor indeed made available to any third party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As we are all academics in this courtroom, don't you regard it as a fundamental mistake not to quote this source you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With one proviso, Your Honour, and it is if the source is not published but a research assistant or associate or collaborator who specifically asks not to be quoted. In other words, let's put it this way: If you are preparing a scientific paper, and you rely on a team of associates or just one or two of them, and they cover certain aspects of an issue -- a discussion, if you use their material, you will not footnote their input if that input is specifically created for the purpose of that paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be then a question of academic honesty to mention those assistants, if they don't want to disclose their identity, by making reference in the beginning or the end of the report, as we normally do it, by thanking those additional sources for their assistance in preparing the report? I can't find anything like this in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have been more than happy to do so were it not for the fact that the aforementioned Dr. Zametica specifically asked me to refrain from doing so in his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in this case, you would mention this person in the form of a pseudonym or circumscribing that there was indeed an assistance from a third side instead of just giving the impression that this would be your own work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I were indicate the assistance of the third party, I would have opened myself to the full disclosure of the identity of the person which would have been the betrayal of trust. Now, unfortunately that trust has been betrayed not due to my own choosing, but due to the fact that obviously the same material was used by another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only the same material, but a full narrative account apparently this very obliging doctor wrote for you and assistant wrote for you and Professor Kecmanovic. This isn't a note, this is a full narrative account.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about one page out of 40. We are also talking about two paragraphs in one instance, and one paragraph in another. I would like to stress that in the context of the fullness of the report including a rather complex attempt to present in a very concise space the roundup of the historical and political sweep of many years and decades, this is not either the main body or the crux or the crucial and essential part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can, and I will, if you insist, take you through all the other pages where there is word for word paragraphs the same. But I just want to know this: Why didn't the doctor want his name mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not for me to comment. I would, since the cat is out of the bag about the research assistance I enjoyed in this respect, I will have to -- yeah, I have a good mind not only to make inquiry of that, but also to make inquiry as to how did it come -- how did the material come to be circulated prior to my use? I wish to assure you once again that had I been not only aware but half suspecting that the access to the material had been made available to another author of expert testimony, I would not have touched it with a barge pole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question on this: Are you proposing to give any of the fee you're going to claim for this report to this doctor?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctor has specifically assured me that my use of the material is on the strictly friendly basis, and that he neither asks nor expects any remunerative package.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We were on page 19. I'm just going to indicate, Doctor, for the benefit of anybody who wants to look at it, there is a passage at the top of "Lost Opportunities for Peace" which is almost identical to that in the professor's report at page 9. The bottom sentence, "once the war broke out in Croatia..." is also identical to part of his report at page 10 and goes over to page 20. Can we go to page 21, please.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your reference in the sentence "In February 1991," to Izetbegovic, "I would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina..." et cetera. And then, "To the Serbs 'this was a war cry...,'" exactly the same quotes appear at page 9 of the professor's report. Now, can we go please, to page 24. In your footnote number 53 on that page, you say -- is that your footnote or the professor's -- the doctor's, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is my own footnote, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "OTP expert witnesses have remarkably little to say about the way events in Prijedor were pushed along by Muslim-Croat initiatives." Which witnesses were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military and Professor Donia in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Were pushed along by Muslim-Croat initiatives from Sarajevo, and this has the unfortunate effect of masking the strictly reactive quality of SDS responses." And that is your opinion, is it, based on your research, your assistant's research and whatever, that the SDS was reacting?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the sequence of events in Prijedor in the period after June of 1991, the first signs of tension were due to the failure of the SDA to accept appointment of the Serb head of the public security station in Prijedor. That was in the summer of 1991. Followed by the tensions in the aftermath of the memorandum on independence vote in the BH assembly. In both cases, the initiatives came from without, in the former case from the MUP headed by Delimustafic and in the hands of the SDA top brass in Sarajevo, and in the latter case, again, as a result of the vote in the republican parliament in Sarajevo. These were not Prijedor initiatives; these were not locally-generated proactive moves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that. What you're saying is that everything that happened, either at the republic level or the local level in Prijedor, in each case, the Serbs are reacting to actions taken by either the Muslims or the Croats, or a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is indeed unsurprising because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't need a further explanation. I just want to know that's your position.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that in most important events, the Serbs seem to take the reactive rather than proactive stance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I want to have a look at one of these reactions that you describe now. Page 27, please, of your report. Now, we looked at this in terms of your footnote from Burg and Shoup, and you say that you made a mistake. It should have been Kumar.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 61.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, 63, in fact.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 63, no. 63 is the quote of Simo Miskovic from Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you looking at page 27 of your report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at footnote number 63 --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- it refers to the setting up of the Herceg Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was your testimony earlier this morning that there was a mistake, instead of ibid, 63, it should be related to Kumar quoted on footnote 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 27 of your report.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 27, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to give us your report, the one that you're looking at. We went through this, and I don't know to go through this again. Yes. Well, you must have made some changes I see here, because the copy that we have is not the same footnote. But it matters not because it's your footnote 61, and I'm somewhat curious as to how we have footnote 63 here, which refers to pages 47 to 48, "after the Croatian community of..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but then we have to go into some details which is the final report in order that we don't have admitted into evidence a wrong report by the expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I understand it, what has been admitted is the one that was filed on the 3rd of March, 2003. However, what Dr. Trifkovic has now showed me is indeed that page, but the footnote is different. It says 61. And what we've all got says footnote 63.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any changes to this report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not since it was submitted. I had this printout from before my trip to the Middle East, which was exactly a month ago today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not at the moment proposing to go through, unless Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, it's for the Defence to clarify this issue, maybe based on a comparison that this report we have before us now ends at page 38 and footnote 101. Apparently some changes have been made in the meantime, and we have to go through this later, but not waste the precious time of the expert. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regardless of whether it's 61 or 63, we dealt with this part. It is a wrong reference. It should not refer to Burg and Shoup. That's what you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pages 47 to 48 from memory, I can say, refers to Radha Kumar's "Divide and Fall."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now would you have a look, please, at page 15 of the Professor's report, where we see that part, the lip service in paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he footnotes it like you, but he gets the right book.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the sequence was changed. There was an inserted footnote in front of the one that came in my use of the Zametica note for the footnote following the plebiscite quote by Miskovic -- or rather, before the plebiscite quote by Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the assertion that both you and the professor make, that "In the same month," you say, "the HDZ set up a Croatian community of Herceg Bosna." What month are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the month of October of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do we see that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. Where in your report do we see the month of October?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference to "everything that was being done was contrary to the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was then in" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause, Doctor. I'm not asking you what was done. I'm asking you where we can find in this paragraph the month "October," because you say "the HDZ ostensible support for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina was but so much lip service. However, because in the same month..."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month refers to the same month when "In this, 'the most delicate question of Bosnian politics,' the outcome of the Assembly session 'hardly reflected the kind of consensus necessary,'" et cetera, which is month of October when the vote on memorandum of independence took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't give a month in that paragraph, do you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the reference to the vote in the assembly was made on the previous page, "on the night of October 14th, 15th, when the SDA and HDZ voted on the memorandum on independence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying in October, the HDZ set up the Croatian community of Herceg Bosna, and then the SDS responded by organising on November 9th to the 10th a plebiscite of its own?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS response was not to any action by HDZ per se. The SDS response was primarily to the assembly vote by the SDA and the HDZ of October 14th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that this -- the response on November 10th, we should not read in conjunction with the community -- I'm sorry, with the HDZ setting up the Croatian community?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it should read: "In conjunction with the vote of the assembly of October 14th, 15th."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you know perfectly well, don't you, that the Serbs couldn't have reacted by the plebiscite of 9th to the 10th, to the setting up of the community of Herceg Bosnia, or Bosna --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which predated -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it did, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The plebiscite came before the setting up?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I am referring to the Serb response as the response to the most delicate of questions of Bosnian politics. In other words, the end of the paragraph referring to the HDZ action is not the one that prompted the Serbian response. The Serbian response in paragraph 2 on this page refers to the SDA/HDZ vote on the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you told us a moment ago that when you said "the same month," you meant October 1991. Because in the same month, the HDZ set up a Croatian community of Herceg Bosna. And that was wrong, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a mistake of the month, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And funnily enough, Professor Kecmanovic made the identical mistake.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I readily admit that the end of this paragraph is entirely the research notes given to me by Dr. Zametica with the assurance that they had been neither circulated nor made public, nor in any way accessible to third parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's totally wrong for anybody to conclude that you copied blindly what the professor had written?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not copying blindly. I was in this respect referring, again looking at the continuation of the sentence, it is very easy to mistake the context of the month. And what I meant to say with the HDZ is the month -- the same month when the Serbs had their plebiscite. The order of the argument should have been reversed. What happened in the month of November are both the Serbian plebiscite and the HDZ declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was the HDZ, as you call it, which responded to the plebiscite held by the Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian decision was not solely the response to the Serb plebiscite. It is also the result of a long-standing policy that was agreed by the Tudjman -- by Tudjman himself and his leadership at a meeting with the Croatian politicians from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb on 10th and 17th of June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I would like you to have a look, please, at a newspaper article from -- this is another one I have difficulty with. Oslobodenje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: While we are conducting this research, may I ask, Doctor, what is your exact time of departure scheduled for today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, in view of the likelihood of the proceedings continuing until the end of the day, I postponed my departure for tonight, and my departure from London for tomorrow morning. So don't feel restrained as far as today's proceedings are concerned. Just I have the request that we don't go beyond the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we would -- sorry to interrupt, but we have to make this scheduling. We have three options. Either we proceed until 1.45, and then from 4.15 to 5.30. This would be the late solution. I think may be better, but it's for the parties to decide. Until 12.30 now, and then continue from 2.00 to 4.30. Or continue now until 1.30, and then from 3.00 to 4.30. Any strong feelings against a solution continuing now until 12.30, and then restarting at 2.00 to 4.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections to this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we continue now until 12.30, and restart at 2.00 until 4.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you got the original article there, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the original, but the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll show you the original so you can confirm that it's... Headed 20th of November, 1991, Self-organisation of Posavina and Herceg Bosna. "Croatian community Bosanska Posavina was founded on the 12th of November, and Croatian community of Herceg Bosna was constituted on the 18th of November in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As it was said yesterday at the regular press conference of HDZ/BH, these are actions of self-organisation of Croatian people, and be it a concrete answer to the formation of the Serb autonomous regions." And I don't think we need to bother about the rest.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But on the other hand, in the entrefilet, formation of interests of the Croatian people, we have "from Mate Boban himself, the opposite view." And I quote: "This is not a reaction to the Serbian plebiscite, but the result of policy articulated by the Croatian democratic community," which is exactly the point I made a minute ago about the policy agreed with Tudjman at the two meetings in Zagreb in June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that it happened approximately a week, in one case two days, after the Serb plebiscite, and in the other case a week, still shows the Serbs reacting against what was initiatives taken by the HDZ. Is that really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying is that the Serb plebiscite cannot be taken as the prompt for the HDZ to act in this way because the plebiscite had a purely informal character of ascertaining the wishes of the plurality of Serbian people without constitutional and legal consequences. In that sense, plebiscite differs from referendum. If one were to give an evaluation of these two apparently contradictory articles, I would say that Mate Boban is probably right when he says that this is not a reaction to the Serbian plebiscite, but the result of a pre-existent Croatian democratic community policy, but that on the other hand, Stjepan Kljuic or whoever issued the other statement may have found it prudent to contextualise the decision with the aftermath of the Serbian plebiscite, and thus to give added justification for something that had been on the cards in any event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, it would be wholly wrong to suggest that you agree with Mate Boban because it fits in with your Serb theory of the events?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, quite the contrary. I think that Mate Boban was probably stating the real state of play when he declared that this was not a reaction to the Serb plebiscite, but the result of the pre-existent HDZ policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which was a reaction to the autonomous regions which had been created some time earlier. That's what the article says.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the formulation of interests of the Croatian people article, Mate Boban is specifically denying that this is the reaction of Serbian plebiscite and asserting real, legitimate, and democratic power of the Croatian community in the BH, which really fits in it with the long-standing position of Mate Boban, that as one of the three constituent nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats should establish and preserve and if possible enhance their political -- collective political individuality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back to what you say --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The article "self-organisation" would be S416A and, the other 417.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just look at your report again, please, at page 27. You say: "The plebiscite showed that whoever represented the majority in Prijedor, it was not the SDA." Why did it show any such thing?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the people who joined in the plebiscite were not only SDS voters; in other words, the number of people who declared themselves in favour of staying within Yugoslavia, because that was ultimately the choice presented to the voters, were people who had supported the League of Communists movement for Yugoslavia, people who belonged to the veterans' associations, people who even didn't declare themselves as Serbs but Yugoslavs in the ethnic sense. What you have to bear in mind in the context of the Prijedorian plebiscite is that it was not perceived as a plebiscite for the greater Serbian option, but rather the plebiscite for remaining part of the joint state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only people, with a few exceptions, who voted in this so-called plebiscite were the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with respect, I would emphasise that according to the census of 1991, a considerable number of the denizens of Prijedor declared themselves as neither Serbs, nor Muslims, nor for that matter Croats, but as Yugoslavs. I do not have the figures in front of me. And many of those so-called Yugoslavs supported the plebiscite as was obvious from the statements and pre-plebiscite proclamations recorded in the Kozarski Vjesnik by the aforementioned organisations that had all Yugoslav rather than ethnically Serb character.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Doctor. Do you accept that in 1991, the Muslims were the majority population in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the census of 1991, yes, I believe the ratio was 51 to 49.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. How is it, then, that a plebiscite voted in by Serbs, and maybe what you call others or Yugoslavs as well, showed that the majority in Prijedor was not represented by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is really quite simple, that at the time of the census, a number of people who did not declare themselves as either Serbs or Muslims or Croats, but Yugoslavs, at the same time voted in the plebiscite in favour of staying with Yugoslavia. I think that for people who called themselves Yugoslav in the ethnic sense, it is unsurprising to choose to stay part of Yugoslavia without necessarily identifying themselves with the SDS cause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to point to the proportion of people who were Muslims who voted in this SDS plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I do have a strong suspicion, however, that among the people who had declared themselves Yugoslavs, we had both Serbs and Muslims. The commitment to the preservation of the common state had been quite strong among that segment of the society in Bosnia-Herzegovina that had strong links with partisan veteran affairs and with the old, by that time, defunct communist party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware, aren't you, that there were two different-coloured ballots for those that voted in the plebiscite, one for Serbs and one for others?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware that there were two separate questions, one for Serbs and one for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, please, then to -- just a moment. Yes, just a note, please, page 26 of your report, "Sovereignty vs. Legality and National Equality." Page 13 of the Professor Kecmanovic's report starts in the same way, headed "Sovereignty and the Constitution." Now, page 29, please, "Proclamation of the Serb Republic." "The formation of autonomous Serbian authorities, far from being the product of a grand design or of an intricate joint criminal enterprise, can be seen both as a necessary response to an emergency and a stance on which to start bargaining." Who asked you to talk about joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one. I am aware of the fact that the proclamation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on January 9th is regarded as a part of the so-called joint criminal enterprise, and I felt that it was indeed appropriate to bring the term in because I believe that the act of January 9th had, again, both reactive character and not a conclusive character, but the character of staking out a position which could be modified as the result of further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The autonomous bodies," that is, the SAOs, "were the result of improvisation is unsurprising, since there had been no agreed SDS master plan of what to do." That's what you assert.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of an SDS master plan, and I think that the almost-stumbling character of the responses, improvised responses, by the SDS in the period of October, November, December of 1991, and January of 1992, indicates rather a hasty and ad hoc attempt to create appropriate responses rather than the following of a long-conceived and well-strategised plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you watch the sentencing of your ex -- I won't say boss, but your ex-associate Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I've seen her statement on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have another look at it, please. I'd like you to have a look, I'm sorry so sorry, the document "The Factual Basis for Plea of Guilty."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know Your Honours I think have it, but we have copies here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object, Your Honour. If this witness will not be called to testify, how would it be possible for us to question anything said in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The point is, Your Honour, is not whether it's what she said, but what his reaction in light of his assertion to what she said is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As it was ruled several times since the beginning of this case, it's the right of the parties, whenever they have a sound basis, then this might be put to the witness. And it's not a question whether the author of this document or this statement will ever testify in this Court. As far as we take into account and have as evidence only the reaction by the expert on this. So therefore, objection dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read this before?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you read it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to me through the Internet shortly after -- I believe it was when her plea was -- sometime last fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before you actually wrote - if that's the right word for your report - before you compiled this report, you knew what she had said as the basis for her plea.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for Mrs. Plavsic's plea is her own sense of the events and her own feeling of remorse for what she had taken part in as she perceived those events to be. Her statement does not contain specific reference to documents or positions adopted by the Serbian -- by the Serbian democratic party leadership that would be indicative of the universal acceptance of her plea as an agreed position of the SDS leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a remarkable sentence if I may say so, Dr. Trifkovic. You assert there is no agreed SDS master plan of what to do.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am specifically --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. That is what you say in your report at page 29.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mrs. Plavsic says, and this is article -- or paragraph 9, that the "meeting was a significant step in the evolution of the general political strategy and objectives..., in particular the determination to create Serbian ethnic territories in BH." That does not to my mind mean that it was agreed at the meeting in the aftermath of the assembly vote to create BH ethnic territories, that it was her sense that this was indeed the objective. These are two different things. And I'm sure you as a lawyer will appreciate that what the Serbs were definitely striving to do is to create political institutions that would give expression to their determination not to be faced with fait accomplis, and not to be taken out of Yugoslavia against their will. Whether Dr. Plavsic perceived such determination to entail the creation of Serbian ethnic territories, implying cleansing of non-Serbs, is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at a different paragraph. Paragraph 10: "The SDS and the Bosnian Serb leadership were committed to a primary goal that all Serbs in the former Yugoslavia would remain in a common state. One method of achieving this goal was by separating the ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. By October 1991, the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mrs. Plavsic knew and intended that the separation of the ethnic communities would include the permanent removal of ethnic populations, either by agreement or by force, and further knew that any forcible removal of non-Serbs from Serbian-claimed territories would involve a discriminatory campaign of persecution." Do you say that that is consistent with your assertion that there was no agreed SDS master plan?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably the most important question posed today. I would be most reluctant to accept that Mrs. Plavsic's account of Serbian intentions is the one that was universally shared by the SDS leadership. If it were indeed established to be so, I would be most distressed to have been ever associated with any of them. However, I have still some faith in the possibility that Mrs. Plavsic's personal account of those proceedings and her sense of what was intended and what was sought is not necessarily the one that would be shared by other members of the SDS leadership, most certainly not those lower on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- I see. You're saying that Mrs. Plavsic made a terrible mistake. All the time during 1992, she was under the impression that there was an agreement in the SDS and the Bosnian Serb leaders to commit these offences but she was totally wrong?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that she was totally wrong. I'm saying that in the fluent situation in which moves are forced by the march of events and often improvised, assumptions are made, unspoken assumptions sometimes, which unless are reflected in the clear documentary evidence may have a Rashomonian to it in the sense of the same set of statements or events meaning different things to different people. And let me remind you that in the period in question, Mrs. Plavsic did have the reputation of a somewhat more excitable member of the Bosnian Serb leadership, certainly she was perceived as one of the more radical ones. It was due to her considerable evolution later on that she was accepted by the international community as a useful interlocutor. I would not like to speculate on the extent to her mistaken belief that this, that, or the other was the agreed policy. I'm simply suggesting that short of a clear set of documentary evidence that would indicate agreed policy of ethnic persecution leading to ethnic cleansing, which she feels guilty of, it would be very difficult for me to accept her statement as, you know, the conclusive proof that such grand master plan was indeed in existence and was universally agreed upon by different parties in the Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I asked you. You're saying, as an excitable member of the Bosnian Serb leadership, she has come away with a totally false impression of the meetings she attended and the instructions that were given. Is that really what you're saying --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally false is a matter of conjunction. I would say that there is no doubt that among the Bosnian Serb leadership, there was an intent in the aftermath of the assembly vote on October 14th to set up political institutions that would give meaning to the political will of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is also no doubt that this intent acquired territorial characteristics through, first, the communities of municipalities, and then the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but those bodies did not preclude a rearrangement of internal Bosnian Herzegovinian constitutional order that would still allow for the continued existence of the republic as an entity. Whether this also entailed the intent to force populations out, to exchange populations, or to otherwise alter the ethnic picture of those territories, I am not fully satisfied on the basis of Mrs. Plavsic's testimony alone that it is an established fact and that it was universally accepted as such by all elements in the Bosnian Serb decision-making structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can't accept it, can you, Doctor, because that would go counter to everything that you have been alleging in this so-called report, the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me finish, please. The Serbs were reacting to events and that there was no grand strategy?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition, I would say that if we look at different elements of the other parties' power structure, most notably, Abdic and Zulfikar Pasic on the Muslim side, we could equally use their statements as the grounds to claim that the Izetbegovic policy had been duplicitous from the beginning and had sought to deprive the Serbs of their constitutional and to establish political mechanisms for their marginalisation that were both unconstitutional and illegal. Statements by direct participants in ongoing events, unless, again, as I mentioned earlier supported by direct documentary evidence have to be compared against other statements. Other statements referring to the problem of policy towards ethnic minorities do not lead me to conclude that there was an agreed and clearly understood SDS policy of altering the ethnic balance by force. If you believe that Mrs. Plavsic's confession of and by itself is sufficient to establish such claim beyond reasonable doubt, I have to beg to differ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do understand the difference, don't you, between a public statement in a newspaper and the basis of a plea of guilty for which Mrs. Plavsic you say, quite wrongly, accepted a sentence of 11 years' imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, quite wrongly, no. I said this statement undoubtedly Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 13883 to 13900. reflects Mrs. Plavsic's heartfelt and sincere impression of those events. What I am saying is that when ascertaining the facts of the case referred to, we have to allow for the possibility that in decisions that often involve implied, not-clearly stated or spelled out or insufficiently clarified elements, we would be on somewhat slippery ground if we took her statement by itself as the clear indication of the existence of a master plan of ethnic cleansing. And I would again submit that I also personally hope that this is not the case; indeed, it is quite possible for different people in the same room listening to the same discussion to have different accounts of that discussion afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, can I just ask you this: What would it take to convince you that there was, in fact, a conspiracy, a joint criminal enterprise, between the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs? What would it actually take to convince you that this happened?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interesting question, and the one that even though probably merits more mature reflection, on an ad hoc basis, I would respond by speculating that a similar confession from another member of the top Bosnian Serb leadership would reluctantly force me to accept that indeed there was a hidden master plan of which they alone were aware at the time. In addition, I believe that may be the emergence of a smoking gun document of some kind, but I would be very surprised if indeed there was intent referred to by Mrs. Plavsic that any such intent would have been codified in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So paragraphs 12 and 13 of what she said, "the SDS prepared and distributed written instructions to SDS municipal leaders to form Crisis Staffs, proclaim Serbian Municipal Assemblies...," et cetera, et cetera. "The municipal Crisis Staffs implemented these objectives and directives in the field, including ultimately the objective of ethnic separation by force." She is just wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not want to mix apples and pears here. We are not now discussing whether she is wrong about the existence of SDS directives. The SDS directives dated December 1991 certainly did exist; so did directives by the other parties, because let us remember, this is the period of the scramble for control. Similar directives existed on the Croatian side preceding the creation of their community. And as far as the SDA side is concerned, the directives issued from the meeting in the police hall in Sarajevo on the 10th of June of 1991 preceding the war in Croatia and Slovenia also had the character of creating parallel power structures, including the political military structures even before -- six months before the events we are discussing right now. So in direct answer to your question, I would say that while it is undeniable that SDS did prepare and distribute written instructions to SDS municipal leaders to form Crisis Staffs, proclaim Serbian Municipal Assemblies, and so on, it did not necessarily follow from this that the intent and the meaning and the purpose of such instructions was as stated in paragraph 10. What I still believe, short of the standard of proof that you have asked me to indicate, is that it is possible that these moves meant different things to different people. And certainly to most Serbs, the intention was not to chase away their neighbours of different ethnicity, but at the same time to remain within the Yugoslav state, either in the Bosnian context, that's end of 1991 and early 1992, or outside that context which was the shift later on in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it ever occur to you to qualify these sweeping generalisations? How do you know what most Serbs wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sweeping generalisations or not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sweeping generalisations have a certain quality to them of reflecting an overall reality, which if we lose ourselves in the minutia of the statements by individuals, we lose sight of. Ordinary people have a tendency, and I'm talking not only of Serbs but Croats and Muslims as well, have a tendency to live in peace and to want peace. If we look at the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the winter of 1991 and 1992, my hunch is - and I say this in full knowledge that a lot of my personal contacts from that part of world have reiterated the same - that most people would have chosen peace, and were prepared to sacrifice some of their political objectives for the sake of peace. But that political leaderships on all three sides were more radical and more determined to pursue their political objectives even at the risk of sacrificing peace. I believe, and I think that events of the post-Dayton period will indicate the same, that faced with a similar choice, most people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if given the means of democratic expression of their views, would rather lower the threshold of their political and constitutional expectations than risk the repetition of the nightmare of 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the summary of this long answer is you don't know what most Serbs wanted, but you're guessing or speculating?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is more than guessing or speculating. It is also supported by the almost universal plea for peace that came from the grassroots in Bosnia in 1991, as the reaction to the war in Croatia and the peace demonstrations in Sarajevo that preceded the collapse into Hobbesian nightmare in 1992. I think it is also a fact well-known in social anthropology that political leaderships, by virtue of being more highly motivated, almost by definition more politicised than the rank and file, also have the exceptions and objectives that tend to be more sharply focussed and more hardline, more extreme, than their rank and file, their overall following.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to respectfully reply to your questions to the best of my ability. If you believe that this is either irrelevant or otherwise inadmissible, I would welcome your comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tempt me, Doctor, but I don't think I will. Can we move or look at your assertions in respect of the October -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I've dealt with the Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May that be made as an exhibit as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm hesitant to have this admitted into evidence because, in fact, we don't know what will be the future. And the evidence we have before us is reflected on the transcript and based on your questions. So therefore, I would rather appreciate not to admit this into evidence in the moment --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll leave that for a later discussion then perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, what you said about the meeting of October the 14th, 1991, which you hold responsible for everything that happened thereafter, was that when the debate was adjourned on the evening -- I'm sorry, I'm looking at page 76 of the transcript of the 13th of March - on the evening of October 14th, "Serbian deputies simply left assuming this was the end of the proceedings for the day. But the Croats and Muslims were surreptitiously informed to reconvene, one might say conspiratorially, and in the middle of the night, and to carry the vote by simple majority." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that the minutes of this meeting is something, one of the few original documents that you've looked at.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to have a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. It may be before it's handed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we can proceed five more minutes. This would be exhibit Number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It hasn't been exhibited before, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Provisionally marked S418.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is part of the minutes of this particular session, if you want to look at the B/C/S version, you may, Dr. Trifkovic. We see that there was the continuation of the session on the 11th of October, 1991. After various speakers, Mr. Azra -- maybe it's a woman actually. Azra Idrizbegovic took the floor and proposed the following to the assembly of the socialist republic, and then we see setting out in the following paragraphs what was set out. And quotes the 60th amendment to the constitution, which was an amendment passed under communist times, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the amendment passed in the dying period of communist rule when the already renamed League of Communists had accepted the inevitability of multiparty elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The amendment, and we quote: "Bosnia-Herzegovina is a democratic sovereign state of equal citizens, the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, and members of other nations and nationalities who live there." It goes on to state, this is the proposed discussion: "Bosnia and Herzegovina shall continue to advocate the survival of the Yugoslav community on new foundations acceptable to all, bearing in mind the ethnic composition of its population, Bosnia and Herzegovina shall not accept any constitutional solution for future Yugoslav community that would not include both Serbia and Croatia..." And so on and so forth. If we go, please, to page 3: "The president of the SRBH assembly Momcilo Krajisnik informed the assembly that the SDS deputies did not agree with the recommendation." And then it was agreed, would you accept, that the assembly -- the session was closed at 23.40. And then -- "continuation of the session on the 14th of October, 1991," if you go, please, to page 4, there were clearly a lot of discussions between the deputies of the various parties, and we see then: "After the break, the chairman informed the assembly that the positions had not been brought into line, i.e., the approaches for decision which were supposed to be adopted at this session were different. Since the positions could not be brought into line, the chairman, Momcilo Krajisnik, closed the session, and the SDS deputies left the meeting." And that was a walkout. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the chairman of the assembly, and I quote from what you just said "closes the session," it is not a walkout. It is the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The walkout is when the session is underway, and the aggrieved party or the aggrieved contingent of deputies walk out in protest, and the session is continued. When the chairman of the assembly closes the session, the departure of deputies is not a walkout. It is the departure following the ending of the session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm just concerned with your description of this conspiratorial, going back into the dead of night meeting. "Irfan Ajanovic then proposed that the assembly adopt a conclusion authorising the assembly vice-president, Mariofil Ljubic, to continue running the session. Since the assembly president had closed the session against the wishes of the deputies, the conclusion was accepted. Since the representatives of one party had abandoned the session, Mariofil Ljubic called a break of one hour in keeping with Article 112 of the assembly rules of procedure." And then we go on, and as you say, the memorandum was passed. Now, where is the conspiratorial sneaking back into the assembly that you've described?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, after the departure of Momcilo -- Momcilo Krajisnik closes the session and the SDS deputies leave the meeting. This is not the abandonment of the meeting, this is not the walkout. These people are under the impression that the meeting is over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the language used here, "closed the session and the SDS deputies left." Now, I would like to know on what basis do you suggest that they abandoned the meeting for which they thought would go on and would continue, when in fact many of them subsequent to these events specifically said that they were under the impression that the meeting was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But may I say, I'm not at this stage entering into an argument of the rights and wrongs of the walkout or leaving or whatever. What I am putting to you, Dr. Trifkovic, is that your description of what happened next then is thoroughly -- to this Court is thoroughly misleading.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that it is quite crucial to understand that the decision, and this is the paragraph that we went on "Irfan Ajanovic then proposed" and so on, that this is in political substance of the Bosnian crisis, one of those thresholds that however innocuous they look when written down and recapitulated more than a decade later, had the momentous effect of incalculable proportions. I am not alone suggesting that by plunging into the vote of this memorandum in the absence of Serbian MPs, the SDA/HDZ deputies raised the threshold, uped the ante, and increased the risk of violent confrontation in the republic. I don't think that this view is something that needs to be greatly elaborated upon. In terms of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian constitutional arrangements and practice, for two ethnic groups to get together and outvote the third, and worse still to vote on a key decision in the absence of a third was simply entering into uncharted waters which until that moment, at least, had retained the constitutional character and the legality of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you finally this: Supposing, as happened, the SDS utterly refused to take any part in assemblies or the vote for the referendum, which I want to come to this afternoon, the vote for the referendum, does that mean that the rest of the other parties would be completely and utterly unable to make a move, in your view?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Law is the law. And if the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina stipulated that consensual participation of the three constituent ethnic groups, or rather their representatives, is required for a key determination influencing the republic's future, the fact that 61 per cent would have favoured a certain option, and that 32 per cent did not, is not by itself sufficient to alter the rule of law. If you, on the other hand, say that in order for the majority to overrule minority, we can and should overlook constitutional niceties, then by the same token, if the Flemings outnumber Vlaamse in Belgium, they may vote to join the Netherlands. If -- you know, examples can go on. The very purpose of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian constitutional arrangement preventing that kind of scenario was to prevent this kind of outcome. I'm not saying whether it was right or wrong or whether it is desirable or to be condemned, I'm simply saying that on the basis of the constitution of 1974, and the amendments of 1990, and the power-sharing agreement on which the political arrangements were made in the aftermath of the November 1990 election, this move was illegitimate, illegal, and unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the answer to the actual question I asked, yes, they could do nothing if the SDS refused to cooperate? Is that the simple answer?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not do what they sought to do. There are all kinds of arrangements that can be made and reached through negotiations. But if you try to impose your will against the constitution, against the law, and against the spirit of political agreement in a very delicate period in time, and try to justify your decision by the plurality of opinion, that means that the rule of law goes out the window. I am very concerned that you suggest that by virtue of having the plurality of opinion in the tactical HDZ/SDA alliance, the deputies for those two parties were justified in violating the republic's constitution and the assembly's procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am purely putting to you, Dr. Trifkovic, that your description of this conspiratorial meeting is misleading, and the second aspect is whether it is your view that the SDS could have gone on, not just in October, but whatever happened thereafter, refusing to cooperate, and as a result, the majority would have been unable to move? Can you just -- is that your view, please? I do not want a long answer.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have two different questions. The first question was whether the two parties would have been unable to move. The second is whether I'm providing a misleading account or not. I don't think I'm providing a misleading account because the Serbs I understand were under the impression that the session would not continue that evening. The substantive issue of the manoeuvreing space is a quite different matter. Had we remained after 14th, 15th of October within the framework of the Bosnian constitution, and the power-sharing agreement, there are all kinds of creative edifices that could have been achieved, as we have seen indeed with the subsequent negotiations both before and after the war. To claim that the only option open at that moment was to pursue outvoting of one party by two other parties is, I think, extremely unimaginative politically and wrong legally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break. The trial stays adjourned until 2.00. But the parties should be advised that we have to impose a time limit that also the Defence has the right to re-examine the expert. We'll meet again at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask, then, how long Your Honour is giving me after lunch? Because obviously I just want to sort out what I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: About 60 to 70 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, please be seated. And, Ms. Korner, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, I want to deal with a couple of matters about the referendum. Before I do that, can you tell us, what is the title of the article that you can't get hold of that you wrote about this Tribunal in March 2000?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't write about the Tribunal. The article was about the aftermath of the Kosovo crisis, and the Web site article that you had printed out was apparently an edit -- the amalgam of my 1996 article and my 1999 article on the aftermath of the Kosovo crisis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2000 article?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe the Kosovo article was 1999, late 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the title of that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember offhand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you about the referendum held by the Serbs, about two aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you, is it the plebiscite or the referendum?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whatever the Serbs held, whatever it's called, on the 10th, 11th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very important distinction because the implications of the term are very different, and I believe that the Serbs never pretended it to be a referendum. A plebiscite has more of a character of declaratory opinion expression, rather than legally and constitutionally binding arrangement that the referendum would imply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But your view is that this plebiscite was the response by the Serbs to the actions taken by the Croats and the Muslim population in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that were it not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Honestly a yes will do. I've got one hour, Dr. Trifkovic, and I'd like to get through a number of topics.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know who Mr. Mirko Pejanovic is?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the presidency in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he's a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he remained, did he not, within the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albeit with the uncertain electoral base. Who he exactly represented as a Serb is frankly a moot point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Have you read his book?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are literally thousands of titles dealing with all kinds of issues that one is bombarded with on a daily basis. This is not the only subject on earth that I have been dealing with in recent years, and certainly not the one that I have been able to devote my undivided attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that you only read and refer to books that coincide with your own views?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. On the contrary. I would be more than happy to take inputs that would try to invalidate my viewpoints. But when it comes to the essential point that we argued about in the earlier session concerning the character of the vote on October 14th, for instance, I haven't encountered --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not. Let's not go back to October the 14th. I'd like to talk about the referendum.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we are looking at time restraints, let us focus on the issues and not on why I have omitted reading Mr. Pejanovic's book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the question is: You don't think it's important to read what a Serb who remained in the government of BiH has to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's the objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic didn't remain. He was newly implemented. He didn't remain. He has never been elected. The form of the question is not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll change the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't think it was important for a balanced objective view that you told the Court you're presenting to have read the memoirs of a Serb who aligned himself with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina? A . This is exactly the problem that I referred to by saying that Mr. Pejanovic had an uncertain electoral base. In the same way Mr. Milosevic appointed a dutifully obedient Albanian to the Yugoslav collective presidency in 1991, his memoirs probably wouldn't be of great deal of interest the students of the Kosovo crisis. Mr. Pejanovic did not represent anyone but himself. His ethnicity is coincidental in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like you to have a look at something he said, please. Page 49 of his book, for which we have copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have also copied, Your Honour, page 23, because of the time constraints, I'm not going to go through that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at page 49, which has been copied, the paragraph which begins: "In the fall of 1991, a delegation of opposition party leaders approached Alija Izetbegovic, then the chairman of the presidency. The SDS had announced its separate referendum on the future of Bosnia held in the form of a plebiscite of the Serb nation. This referendum was held on the 9th and 10th of November, and the results favoured Bosnia's remaining in rump Yugoslavia. Our delegation," and he names them, "talked long and hard with President Izetbegovic. We hoped to persuade him to somehow pre-empt this step by the SDS which we considered an unconstitutional act and defiance of parliament's authority. After a long discussion, however, President Izetbegovic said finally there was nothing left to be done, and that he saw no possibility of taking further steps to prevent the SDS from holding their referendum. He then suggested that we ourselves should try to do something that we finally agreed amongst ourselves that we could do still less. By this referendum, the SDS ensured support for its aim of using force to bind Bosnia to Yugoslavia." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What specifically? Quite a few statements are contained in the paragraph that you have read. First of all, I do not agree that it was the Serb referendum. Certainly the Serbs did not refer to it as such. And as I indicated earlier, the referendum has very different constitutional connotations to a plebiscite --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause, there, please, he does actually say "held in the form of a plebiscite."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is very different to saying "plebiscite." If you say "a referendum held in the form of a plebiscite" is different to calling it a plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll specifically ask you: Do you agree with him that this step by the SDS was an unconstitutional act in defiance of parliament's authority?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After October 14th, everything is unconstitutional and extraconstitutional, as I said in my own report. But to say this plebiscite is in defiance of parliament's authority and the parliament itself had already violated the constitution and the political agreements through the vote of October 14th is somewhat preposterous. The parliament had effectively negated its authority in the acts of the SDA/HDZ vote on the memorandum on independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do agree, therefore, that it is as I understand it, it was unconstitutional, but you disagree with "in defiance of parliament's authority"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that "by this referendum, plebiscite," I understand what you're saying, "the SDS ensured support for its aim of using force to bind Bosnia to Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is definitely a statement of opinion and not a fact. There are any number of cutoff points on all three sides which could be retroactively regarded as steps leading to violence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move, then, please to the referendum -- actually called the referendum that was held by the Bosnians. You said in your report, and I'll just find the page, page 31 of your report, the referendum, which by the way I think is another one where you and --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overlap because of the resource to the same background study, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "The Serbs boycotted en masse, but the SDS nevertheless made no attempt to block the referendum." Do you mean by that that they made no attempt to prevent Serbs taking part in it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It worked both ways. On the one side, the Serbs did not actively try to prevent the voting in the referendum of the other two ethnic groups. On the other side, and specifically in the Prijedor Municipality, for which I looked at the list of electoral places or voting booths, polls, sorry, there was a deliberate exclusion of majority Serb areas, or rather the polls were not even opened in the majority Serb areas. I think that both sides regarded the referendum as a form of plenary declaration of intent by the Croats and Muslims and the one with which the Serbs did not want to be involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that deliberately, a deliberate exclusion from majority Serb areas or polling stations.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent it was a general occurrence in Bosnia, but there is a document from the Kozarski Vjesnik that actually lists the voting locations in Prijedor which seems to indicate that not the entire territory was covered, and that there was a correlation between the areas which are more heavily Serb-inhabited, and which did not have open polling places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you looked at no documents in relation to this that were sent by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is correct, I did not see documents sent by the SDS vis-a-vis the obstruction of the referendum or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you now, please, to have a look at a document from the SDS dated the 19th of February, 1992, and an accompanying document headed "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 19th of February, 1992, Sarajevo. To the municipal boards and the regional boards: Subject: Standpoints in connection with the referendum delivery. In the enclosure we send you the conclusions of the assembly." And we have that as the next document. "You are obliged at once to hold an expanded meeting of your municipal board which should be attended by all SDS/BH personnel in municipal organs or authority and also meetings of local boards of the SDS all with the purpose of acquainting the Serbian people with the materials we are sending you. "You are obliged to draw up a plan of action so that any kind of campaign to organise a referendum should be made impossible from the point of view of preventing any possible manipulation of the Serbian people. It should be explained to every adult Serb that not only should he or she refrain from taking part in the referendum as a voter, but neither a member of a municipal or any other commission connected with the referendum. It should be explained to our personnel in municipal and other organs of authority that they are not obliged to provide either materials or any other resources for implementation of the referendum or to be involved in it in any form at all. It can be expected that after the adoption of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which will soon be done, the referendum will be illegal on our Serbian sovereign territory, and as such, will not be able to be held." Now, would you say that that was an attempt to prevent Serbs taking part in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An attempt to prevent strictly by political means. I think that the crucial part in what you have just quoted is "you're obliged to draw up a plan of action so that any kind of campaign to organise a referendum should be made impossible from the point of view of preventing any possible manipulation of the Serbian people." It should be explained. In other words, I do not think that in what you have just quoted, there is any implication on the call to coercive, let alone violent measures in order to prevent the holding of the referendum. Strictly persuasion, campaigning, but no, I do not see this as the SDS readiness to resort to coercion and violence in order to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As I say, we have, Your Honour, the actual decision of the assembly to be attached, but I don't propose to go through it, which can be handed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be provisionally marked S420.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it can be given to everyone, but I don't propose to go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Previously some pages of the book provisionally marked as S419.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want you to look at another document, please, in respect of no coercion or anything like that. I'd like you to be handed, please, this document. It comes from the SDS in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the document is from Bosanska Krupa, we think it is outside of the scope of the indictment, and as we know, we tried to introduce a few documents from other municipalities. We are not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't have for one moment gone outside the municipality if it hadn't been for Dr. Trifkovic's assertions in his report and now repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nevertheless, maybe it's possible for you that we have only the answers by the witness or the expert as evidence that we indeed avoid contradictory decisions on the admission of evidence. Please understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't know there was a contradictory decision on this. But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the past, several times it was ruled that we should refrain from discussing other municipalities because, no doubt, the actual situation could be and in fact was different from municipality to municipality. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps I can just --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, just have a look at this document, would you. In the light of that document, do you want to change your answer that there was no coercion and no threats being made to stop Serbs voting?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I see no reason to change my statement. This is a somewhat clumsily worded and emotionally put together, but pretty much standard statement of the Serb position. In the location of the curse of Lazar obviously has the character of a strong emotional appeal. I do not see that it contains either implied or let alone explicit threat of violence against anyone defying the call for boycott. If this kind of language circulated in Bosnia as it did on all sides in late 1991 and early 1992, it is a reflection of the republic's collapsed social and political structure, not of the specific violent intent of the perpetrators. In addition, you admit yourself that this is the document issued by the municipal board of a particular locality, and not a pan-Bosnian SDS document that followed similar language and similar emotional invocations in trying to prevent the Serbs from voting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leaving that aside, Doctor, whether this is Krupa or some other municipality, are you saying that in your view the sort of language used here, and the quotation of the curse of Lazar, would not have an effect on your -- the peasant-type Serb who might have been considering voting?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you're trying to proceed from the particular to the general, and to say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, would a particular Serb, a peasant Serb --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, particular being Krupa in this instance. Now, if first of all we establish that the Krupa leaflet is indeed a typical characteristic illustrative form of appeal on the Serbs not to vote, that was to be encountered all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would appreciate if you would really give me the equivalent example from Prijedor. The second part of your question is, yes, it would appeal on the emotional basis and the political basis. I would not see this as a threat to one's physical security if the call was defied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, such a document was not intended to terrify Serbs and prevent them from voting in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cultural analysis of the language, in particular the curse of Lazar, has the character of shaming them into not voting even if they had considered doing so, which in substantive political terms overwhelmingly, they were not even tempted to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I would like then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Your Honour doesn't want it made an exhibit, then I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, for principle reasons, let us not admit this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
