utterances.text: All right. Now, can we move, please, to page 32 of your report. Paragraph, third paragraph on that page in the end, 62.68 per cent is -- no doubt you've looked at this over lunch -- you'll agree identical to paragraph 51 of Professor Kecmanovic's report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we have already agreed at the beginning of dealing with this section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think we looked at this section before.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the referendum, when we read the previous page and you made the same reference, and I readily conceded that this is indeed so. So short of making another rhetorical restatement of the agreed-upon point, I don't see any reason to dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the line, then, in the next paragraph of your report, the last sentence on that page: "But this did not stop the rump government of Alija Izetbegovic from declaring independence on the 3rd of March."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is taken, according to your report, and --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Professor Kecmanovic's report, it's from Woodward?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Woodward gives no source for this assertion. Would you agree? Would you like to look at the book?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an assertion in -- I believe that it is the language that gives it the character of the assertion. But that, (a), we had the rump government minus the SDS contingent; and (b), that on the basis of the referendum, the proclamation of independence went ahead regardless. Whether it is assertion, whether it's an opinion, whether it is an expression of considered judgement, we may agree to disagree or agree to agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that there was a declaration of independence on the 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a cocktail in the Bosnian presidency that had the character of the formal enactment of independence in the aftermath of the referendum, and the day has been regarded as the holiday by the -- by the internationally recognised Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand the importance of using accurate terms, don't you, to describe events?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have described what happened on the 3rd of March as a declaration of independence by Bosnia and Herzegovina picking that up in Woodward. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like you please to have a look at some of the documents in relation to that so-called declaration of independence. First, can you look at the -- something called the Sluzbeni list. I'm no doubt pronouncing that wrongly. Again, we've got --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we first of all, hand it out. Your Honour, we'll have to put it on the ELMO. My fault. We had a slipup of some of the copying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can probably tell us what the Sluzbeni list?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sluzbeni list, Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that show that on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not working. Is Your Honours' working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not in the moment. I'm trying to do my very best. Judge Argibay's is not working as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think any of ours is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So here we are. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an announcement pursuant to Article 28 of the results of the referendum dated the 6th of March, 1992. Agree?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three days after you say there was a declaration of independence.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately following the closing of the polling booths, there was a celebratory atmosphere in the BH presidency and the declaration that the referendum was a success. If you look at the actual sequence of events in the aftermath of the closing of the booths, the statement in the Official Gazette was only retroactive confirmation of what had already been proclaimed to be a political fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question, and you know it isn't, Dr. Trifkovic. That was not -- whether there was celebrations going on, that was not an official declaration of independence, was that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody realised that with the aftermath of the referendum, the rump leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina had regarded the fait accompli of rounded up. I would really appreciate that instead of invoking the statement in the Official Gazette that was really neither here nor there by the 6th of March when independence was regarded as finished and completed fact by all sides, whether they agreed with it or disagreed with it only detract us -- distracts us from the political substance of the issue which is the character of the referendum, the intent of those who called it, the intent of those who boycotted it, and its consequences. This document, the Sluzbeni list, Official Gazette, giving particular breakdown of the figures for the referendum is furthermore still indicative of the fundamental political point that it did not have the two-thirds majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand what the term "declaration of independence" means?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be very specific. You may declare independence without enacting it in the legal constitutional document that is sealed and stamped. You can declare it verbally in front of TV cameras and in front of the invited diplomatic core and correspondence, or else you can do it with all the paraphernalia of the constitutional format. Either way, the substance of the aftermath of the referendum in Sarajevo had the character of the rump leadership proclaiming independence. Whether that proclamation was couched - and by the way, we are looking at everything in this area being on the other side of constitutionality, because we are looking at two sides acting in concert against one - but be that as it may, we are looking at the substantive issue of the aftermath of the referendum being regarded as irrevocable proclamation of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the rump leadership in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you about this, Dr. Trifkovic, is effectively, because I suggest that what's emerging from this is that either you didn't write this report at all, or if you did write it or some parts of it, you didn't bother to check any facts at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly are you alluding to? The fact that the referendum held on 29th of February and 1st of March did not have the legality and constitutional backing? Or the fact that it was the 1st of March that the de facto proclamation occurred? Please clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the declarations of independence issued by Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any such document at this period of time issued by Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have read the articles in the Oslobodenje on the 2nd of March of 1992 triumphantly proclaiming the independence and quoting top leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the same effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like you to have a look, please, at what Mr. Karadzic had to say about this in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not to lose track, the last conclusions were S420-1 because they belonged to the previous document. The document we can now see on the screen would then be provisionally S421A and B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read these assembly -- this record of this assembly?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which assembly this refers to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at the B/C/S version attached to the back, you'll see a front page saying "minutes and tape recording (transcript of the RS national assembly 17th session on the 24th to the 26th of July, 1992)."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen these minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go, please, to page 3 of the English translation, and of course you're welcome to check it as against the B/C/S. The paragraph that begins: "The characteristics of the external political situation of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina is as follows: By the will of this assembly, we have proclaimed our republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, organised it. Thus, when we saw that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be recognised, we proclaimed our independence a few hours before the independence of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Although BH had never proclaimed independence, but simply submitted a request to the European Community to be recognised, we proclaimed our republic independent." And that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And perfectly in line with what I stated earlier, that there was no formal proclamation of independence adorned with the constitutional framework of the Croatian and Slovenian one, but that in substantive political terms as I stated very clearly, the statements by the leaders in the aftermath of the referendum had the same political effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your view, is it, that your sentence and Professor Kecmanovic and Ms. Woodward, this did not stop the rump government of Alija Izetbegovic from declaring independence accurately describes what we have just been through?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be gratefully appreciative if you would elucidate me what exactly is Izetbegovic's, Ganic's, and others meaning when they say that with the result on camera and in print, that with the result of the referendum, the requirement for independence by the international community has been satisfied, and indeed the subsequent treatment of the date by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the independence day. Now, while I agree with you that the formal declaration in the sense of the Croat and Slovene one of 25th of June was lacking, in terms of substantive actions having clearly defined political consequences, there can be no doubt that indeed a proclamation it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's your answer. Thank you. And now finally, because to finish this, can you look, please, at your report at page 34. You were talking about, in paragraph 34, the EC -- I'm sorry, paragraph 3 on page 34, "The EC recognition ignored -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina ignored its own Badinter Commission which had stipulated that a vote on independence would be valid only if respectable numbers from all three communities approved." Again, this assertion appears at page 31 of Professor Kecmanovic's report. And the source for this, again, is Ms. Woodward.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition, I think if we look at the source document prepared by the Badinter Commission in October of 1991, I believe that the very phrase "respectable numbers" or "convincing segment of each ethnic community" is referred to. What I believe was not the intention of the Badinter Commission when it issued its opinion was a simple outvoting of two ethnic groups by another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at opinion number 4, please, of the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not Ms. Karper's fault, as you can imagine, I have skipped a number of documents that I was going to put. Your Honour, we've stapled together all the opinions, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That we don't lose control once again, the last draft translation was S422, and now it's provisionally S423.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour will find number 154, opinion number 4. You will see -- unfortunately this was a photocopy of my copy. I wrote over the top December instead of November because in the original French which I have here or maybe have been copied for you, that's what it says. And somebody has translated December into November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like you please, to have a look, Dr. Trifkovic, at the last part of opinion number 4. It says: "4, in these circumstances, the arbitration commission is of the opinion that the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute the SRBH as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to be fully established. This assessment to be reviewed if appropriate guarantees were provided by the republic applying for recognition, possibly by means of a referendum of all the citizens of SRBH without distinction carried out under international supervision."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I don't want to give evidence, but if Your Honours look at the French version of this, it says -- the actual wording is I think you'll see "without any distinction." I don't know. Did we provide Your Honours with the French version? We did. If Your Honours look at that, it's the very last page. It hasn't gone into the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where do you see anything about a respectable majority?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because you have focussed now only on the opinion number 4, and I would like to refer you to opinion number 2, which says that "where there are one or more groups within a state constituting one or more ethnic, religious, or language communities, they have the right to recognition of their identity under international law, norms of international law requests states to ensure respect for the rights of minorities," et cetera, et cetera. What you would like to do I suppose is to look at opinion number 4, Article number 4, in isolation from the previous opinions. The -- since opinion number 2 specifically talks about the expression of the political will of the communities, I do not think that we can look at the just-quoted opinion in isolation from the rest. If you're saying that simple majority is what Badinter had in mind, then that opinion would seem to contradict his previous ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Trifkovic. It really was a very simple question. You say, Professor Kecmanovic says, and I imagine Ms. Woodward does, that "The EC recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina ignored its own Badinter Commission, which had stipulated" - do you understand the word stipulate - "that a vote on independence would be valid only if respectable numbers from all three communities approved." Can you tell us, please, where in any of these opinions you find a stipulation to that effect?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stipulation I find in the opinion number 2, which says that it is established that whatever the circumstances, the right to -- "When there are one or more groups within a state constituting one or more ethnic, religious, or language communities, they have the right to recognition of their identity, the norms of international law require states to ensure respect for the rights of minorities, requirement applies to all republics vis-a-vis the minorities, the Serbian population of Bosnia and Herzegovina therefore must be afforded every right according to minorities on international conventions as well as national and better national guarantees consistent with the principles of international law and the provisions of Chapter 2 of the draft convention," and so on and so on. What they refer to is international convention on human rights which establishes the right to self-determination. If the one ethnic community is to be denied the right to self-determination under opinion 2, that would seem to constitute a requirement of the participation of all three ethnic groups, and the expression of the agreement of at least some segment of those three ethnic groups in the change of the constitutional status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you one more time.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, where do you see any stipulation anywhere in those words, that is, "only a vote on independence would only be valid, would be valid only if a respectable number from all three communities approved"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formulation that is quoted in the report and in Woodward is derived from opinion number 2, it is not explicitly per se contained in it and is therefore not quoted in parenthesis. But it is clear from opinion number 2 that "the constituent nation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is entitled to the respect for the principle of the right to self-determination," article number 3 of opinion number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you see a vote on independence in article 2?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, article 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Opinion 2, sorry.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, you're asking first of all for a commentary on opinion number 4, article 4, and what I pointed out is that opinion 4, article 4 should be looked at in conjunction with opinion 2, articles 2 and 3. I am not saying that either article 2 and 3 in opinion 2 by themselves, or article 4 in opinion 4 by itself, is sufficient to provide the answer to your question. But that the two in conjunction have a clear meaning of requiring the participation of the Serbian -- specifically in this case, Serbian community which is entitled to the principle of the right of self-determination that safeguards human rights and so on and so on. If we look at article 4 of opinion 4 of and by itself, without reference to opinion number 2, then indeed, it would appear that no such requirement is present. I would submit that on the basis of opinion 2, it was not the intention of the Badinter Commission that an ethnically-neutral simple majority vote in the referendum would indeed suffice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you don't regard that sentence as misstating the true position?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not misstating; possibly overstating. But not misstating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is because you didn't bother to check that Woodward's reference was correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. I am well familiar with the Badinter findings and recommendations and as you may have seen, I have immediately referenced opinion 4 to opinion 2 because I believe that subsequent opinions of Badinter did not abrogate previous ones, but incorporated them into rather than replaced the previous opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Trifkovic, is the article that you were talking about on Kosovo, was that actually published in Liberty?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, if it was in Chronicles website, it would have been published in chronicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's an article that we didn't have much difficulty in getting from Liberty dated November the 10th, 1999, by you with the title "Kosovo: Invented Massacres."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been taken from the Chronicle's website by the editors of Liberty without my being aware of it, but at the same time I am pretty certain I didn't specifically write the article for Liberty to start with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know if this is the article you're referring to, the one that you say was amalgamated with your 1996 article?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't had copies made yet, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not the amalgamated article. This is another article which has the character of press compilation from a variety of published sources, not -- frankly, this was actually an article in the character of press review rather than an opinion piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you saying this is not an article you've written; this is another compilation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at what this says is the quotes from the El Pais followed by the quotes from Richard Gwyn in Toronto Star, the Daily Mirror, this is what one would call the press review. And this is a Chronicles website segment which deals with the reporting of the foreign press. And I believe that this article was copied from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's not the article you were talking about either?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the article that was incorporated into the website composite that you presented me with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can give that back. Now, finally, I thought that was the final thing, but there's one other matter I want to put to you. You asked me for the evidence that suggested that by October 1992, when Dr. Stakic was giving this interview to the press, most of the Muslims had already left. I'd like you to have a look at a document, please, which was -- it's a 65 ter number 378.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't actually think it has been exhibited yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be provisionally marked S424.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document apparently addressed to the SMB sector of the Banja Luka CSB. Mr. Jelisic is the operative, and the date is the 23rd of October, 1992. Could you look, please, at the part of this report that begins: "From then until today, the consequences of these conflicts can be felt everywhere. Dozens of villages have been almost completely destroyed and left uninhabited, and it lists those villages." "This destruction saw the beginnings of the mass exodus of both Muslims and Croats. According to estimates, roughly 38.000 Muslim and Croat citizens have left the Municipality of Prijedor so far." Do those names mean anything to you, of those places that were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were mentioned in connection with the early clashes and in -- some of them are not. But in order to clarify my answer, first of all, in answer to your question, I did not deny that a large number of Muslims had left at the time of Bishop Komarica's visit. I really don't know where did you get the idea that I needed convincing that this was indeed the case. What I stated explicitly is that the exodus of non-Serbs notwithstanding Dr. Stakic's statements in the period under review displayed consistent spirit of conciliation regardless of the vagaries of events with which he was or was not connected, but certainly did not appear to have reflected his willful commitment and his personal desires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggested to you that by October 1992, when Dr. Stakic was giving this interview, he could, of course, talk about ethnic agreement or whenever the expression was, because by then, there were hardly -- not that many Muslims left in Prijedor. Can you just look at what this operative says at the top of page 3. "As time goes by, one can feel that both the official authorities and the citizens themselves are relaxing under the impression that with the departure of the Muslims and Croats, everything has been accomplished."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly a very condemning statement by the individual concerned. I do not know who it is. As it stands, in my objective opinion, this is a very embarrassing and highly culpable statement that implies his certainly very clear commitment to the kind of policy that if established to have reflected the general policy would be highly compromising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still think that you were better off reading articles in Kozarski Vjesnik and books by Muslims than actual original documents relating to the period?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unfortunate that this particular document, for instance, is not as far as I can tell -- had not been made available to anyone, let alone myself, until this very moment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll leave aside your allegation, Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an allegation. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. And the Defence would confirm what Dr. Stakic is claiming. We have never seen this document before -- Dr. Trifkovic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll repeat again. It was disclosed to the Defence on the 14th of February, 2002. It contained -- it has the 65 ter number 378. I would invite the Defence before leaping to their feet and supporting Dr. Trifkovic's allegations to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, if the Prosecution would be so kind and explain when they gave to the Defence documents marked today as S421, S420, and the rest of the documents submitted today, whether they have those documents or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, none of those, the documents, if they already had been disclosed, we would have given the 65 ter number. They are absolutely right, because nobody thought that these documents were at all relevant until Dr. Trifkovic appeared with this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is the purpose for cross-examination, to cover all the elements covered by the examination-in-chief. And therefore, I can't see anything wrong with this. But let's, please, refrain from discussing the admission into evidence for the moment. The time is absolutely precious.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have, in fact, concluded my cross-examination of Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fast track: When have you been the last time in the area of former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me, Your Honour. On Monday of last week for one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever been in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever try to get access to archives, be it in Banja Luka or be it in Prijedor, in order to have a more complete picture of that what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made clear to me by the Defence team that the only documents that I could process that would be acceptable by the Court are the ones that have been officially translated - I'm talking about the documents that are in Serbo-Croatian in original - and here have been presented to the Court. However, in answer to your question, I haven't had access directly to the archives of the Republika Srpska, and I am not even aware of the freedom of public access in view of the fact that considerable segment of those archives are held as documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever try to get access to these documents? Because as an expert, no doubt, it's not only your right but wouldn't it be also your obligation to try to get access to more contemporanian documents or witness evidence or any additional sources, being more reliable than newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour will remember that the title of the report was "Events in Prijedor in the Context of the Bosnian Crisis." My intent was not so much to analyse the events in Prijedor per se, but to place them in the broader context and to examine them to the extent that the events in Prijedor can be looked at in isolation from the broader events that were shaping Bosnia-Herzegovina politics and society. In that sense, my conclusion from page 35 on seeks to round things off by basically claiming, and I would submit establishing, that Prijedor of and by itself is not a microcosm that it shared the destiny of the rest of the republic through events that were outside the control of any one person or institution within the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Related to your working method, it's absolutely correct what you are stating, that it's practice to send around a kind a few questionnaire or ideas asking friends, colleagues whether they could attribute something to the ideas of a draft. You have a concrete list of recipients of these documents whenever you try to get -- or to prepare an academic work?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the area of concern, and quite obviously different people would be the recipients for different aspects. Let me reiterate that my initial speculation on this subject was due to my being genuinely puzzled at the overlap with Dr. Kecmanovic's report which only became clear to me when I realised that the reliance on the same set of background notes from the same source was obviously utilised by both authors, Dr. Kecmanovic and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you stand by your testimony that you, in fact, sent around these first ideas --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, most certainly. And I am not saying now that the overlap was due to that circulation. I am now convinced that in fact, the same set of notes from the same source had been passed on to both Kecmanovic and myself, and that my understanding that these were pro bono friendly sets of notes to be used without retribution as I deemed fit was the source of both confusion and embarrassment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This list of recipients, these were only Serbs or did you ask also your Muslim colleagues or Croat colleagues?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, most of my requests for comments and opinion would be to people who have no ethnic connection with that part of the world, specifically because I believe that it is sometimes necessary to have no ethnic axe to grind in order to have the distance and the detachment necessary for a cool-headed assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you share the view that there is not one historical truth at all?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an extremely intriguing question and the one that calls for a complex answer, and I'm afraid we probably don't have time for that. I would say that there is the evolving truth and that a good example would be, for instance, the diplomatic history of the outbreak of World War I, which -- the July crisis of 1914 which has had different stages of evolution and analysis over the past 80-odd years. I would say that in human affairs, there is no single truth cast in stone and established for all times, that dependent on both the emergence of new evidence and the new angles of analysis and inquiry, each generation will throw new lights and events. Otherwise, once written, history would be immoveable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a conference of representatives, put it this way, of all areas, say, from Slovenia, from Croatia, from Serbia, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, coming together, try to find the lowest common denominator where you could say "this is the fundamentum on which we can build together"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have attended a number of such conferences which, however, did not have such a broad sweeping objective as you have indicated, Your Honour. Specifically, it was under the auspices of AAASS, American Association for the Advancement of Slavic Studies. Because they operate on the basis of panels, I have taken part in panels where people of different backgrounds and different opinions on the aspects of the wars on former Yugoslavia would meet in the spirit of collegial disagreement very often, but always in terms of academic discourse and even the ability to communicate in a friendly manner in the social context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you regard it as an agreed fact that by the end of June 1999, there was a five-day war by the JNA occupying the Slovenian borderlines?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. End of June.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in June is I would call it a tremendous blunder by ineptly- and ideologically-motivated leadership of the JNA. I would not even dignify it with the term "war" because a war entails clear strategic plan and end game and objectives and exit strategies, which in the case of frankly criminal but totally inept ad hoc and misguided intervention of the JNA in Slovenia would not be even dignified by such name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you agree that one could have a second, separate period of time, until January 1992, being an open war escalating in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "war" is much more applicable to the Croat situation with the proviso that there was no complete identity of either interests or intentions between the JNA, which was still in existence at that time, and the local Serb militias and Territorial Defence units, refusing to recognise the control of central Croatian authorities. In fact, if we look at the pattern of JNA garrisons surrendering and evacuating from Croatia in the Serbs' minds, and I'm talking about the Krajina Serbs, there was a great deal of distrust of what they regarded as ideologically motivated JNA and its apparent reluctance to commit itself to the defence of Serb interests. It's only with the emergence of the so-called army of the Serbian Krajina that the dichotomy was at least ostensibly eliminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you call it as an agreed fact that the JNA, after returning from Croatia, primarily settled in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true that from this period on, say until autumn 1992, we could speak about a third war with about 200.000 victims on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one date in that period which we nevertheless need to mention, if at least in passing, and it is May 19th of 1992, and the departure of non-Bosnian personnel of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's concomitant leaving behind of a significant part of its weaponry and materiel behind. To what extent is there a continuity between the JNA and the VRS, and to what extent is the command and control structure of both structures -- of both bodies essentially the same is a matter that historians need yet to establish with complete certainty. I personally think that the lines of command in the case of the VRS always extended up all the way to Belgrade, even though the fact was not completely apparent to the personnel on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for a moment of thinking, if you would have been approached in the past by, say, Mr. Milutinovic, or just another example, by Mr. Hadzihasanovic, asked for an expertise as you did it for Dr. Stakic, would you have done this?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I would have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why this?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I would have strong moral qualms taking part in any effort dealing with the members of a power structure that I regard as deeply flawed and unfortunate for the scenarios unfolding in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s. When it comes -- and obviously, Mr. Milutinovic is inseparable from the Milosevic establishment. My record of writing and public commentary on the Milosevic regime in Belgrade is both long and a matter of public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that you visited twice Dr. Stakic in the United Nations Detention Unit. Was this to experience or to find out whether or not both of you were more or less of one and the same political opinion?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was very little talk of politics per se. My specific intent was to personally satisfy my own curiosity as to the character and, if I can use the colloquial term, the vibes, the aura of the man, and my own sense of his sincerity in his claim that he neither knew, nor wanted, to support the events of which he is accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you as an academic normally check your sources on the question of reliability?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, this was something very different to what would be the normal academic routine because it entailed a personal engagement in a matter that obviously touches upon one's own values and one's own conscience. For instance, referring to the newly disclosed document, I would have been extremely unhappy if the quote at the top of page 3, and I am now being very sincere with you even without your prompting, if such a document were to be found to have been signed by Dr. Stakic. I would have been both disappointed and defeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you agree with a sentence stating: "Muslims who were created artificially"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have a problem with the term "Muslims" for the ethnic group that now refers to the Bosniaks. I think that their emergence as a separate ethnic group is the product of a spontaneous ethnogenesis over a period of centuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt, you are trying to avoid a clear answer. Once again, would you agree with the sentence: "Muslims who were created artificially"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever crosscheck and try to find out to what extent Kozarski Vjesnik was a reliable source, apparently the only source, despite of those other quotations you made or others made it for you? Did you ever contact anybody from Kozarski Vjesnik, and the role Kozarski Vjesnik played in 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozarski Vjesnik in my considered opinion is a reliable and objective source until the spring of 1992. And after that date, it becomes more or less a one-party mouthpiece of the SDS ruling establishment in Prijedor, which is why I relied upon it mostly in the period of its multiethnic editorial board and composition of reporters, whereas I only used factual reports with direct quotes such as, for instance, the one concerning the visit by Bishop Komarica in the period thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But the conclusion would be that in the period following, say, April 1992, summer 1992, you would admit yourself that you didn't have any really reliable sources?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in any event, Your Honour, my report ends with the spring of 1992 in any event. And from that point on, we enter into the area of military report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. So in conclusion, you never tried to get access via the Defence or other sources to other, be it documents, be it audiotapes, be it videotapes reflecting that what has been stated in the period of time you covered with your report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supplied with a considerable wealth of additional supplementary documents concerning primarily Oslobodenje daily, Dani magazine, and Slobodna Bosna, as well as by the memoirs of a total of four Bosnian army commanders who were active in the early days of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you agree that these are secondary sources only?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are absolutely secondary sources, I agree. But at the same time, it is the secondary sources that for the broadbrush outline of the political context of developments within which the Prijedor episode was unfolding are more suitable than the primary sources which may be individually useful elements in the mosaic, but which need hundreds or even thousands of such little stones in order for the mosaic to be intelligible. And that is something that I had neither time nor resources to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is your work directly or indirectly, maybe via one of the chronicles you're editing, funded by a third source?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely not?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The only funding such as it was in the form of modest advance came from the Defence team and from no third party whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was a more general question --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- related to the period of time since 1992.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't understand the question. Can you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there any kind of funding of your work, by whomsoever, since 1992, be it directly or indirectly by, for example, supporting the editing of articles or chronicles or whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean am I paid for my writing for Chronicles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I asked whether you received any fundings which would not be in a kind of duo des [phoen] related to concrete articles or chronicles, but a general political support, and thereby, because all support, first of all, needs money, did you receive any money in support of your work?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In support of my work, in the spring of 1994, I did receive a small financial support during the period of my attempts to set up the Republika Srpska representative office based in London. That was the only outright grant per se. Other than that, all of my work, journalistic, academic, and otherwise, was on strict either salary or contract or consultancy basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you received this financial support by whom, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the members of the Serbian diaspora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you also add names to this?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were events such as dinners or open events where collections would be made which would generally be accounted for through the acquisition of equipment and the related expenses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, during your testimony on Friday, you stated that - it is page 13.647 and 13.648 LiveNote - you stated that, Following in Pasic tradition meant to give expression to ethnic particularism within the Yugoslav framework, and I emphasise not only that that would give expression to the Serb particularism, but also other groups. In this regard, I would like to ask you, are you aware that Nikola Pasic interpreted the idea of the Slavs unity and the ethnic particularism within this unity in a way that would ensure Serbian supremacy, and that he during all his life did his best to implement this idea along the lines of a Great Serbian concept?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in answer to your question, it would be necessary to emphasise that Pasic's views were evolving. What you're referring to is probably accurate, talking of the closing months of World War I, when Pasic changed his mind about the Corfu declaration of 1917, and insisted that the submersion of Serbia into the Yugoslav project without the clear delineation what belonged to whom, so to say, was a mistake. However, in the course of the early 1920s, and especially in the course of his attempts to reach an agreement and an understanding with the Croat peasant party of Stjepan Radic, Pasic was forced to modify his views especially in view of the fact that Regent Aleksandar, later King Aleksandar, opted for the unitarist constitution, the so-called Vidovdan constitution of 1921, and that Pasic was obliged to act within its brief and within its restraints. So in answer to your question, the answer is that had Pasic had the full choice of political options in the course of negotiations with the Yugoslav committee during World War I, he would have preferred to define the Serbian lands first and then to unify them with Croat and Slovene ones, but within the restraints of post-World War I arrangements, Pasic was forced to modify his views and furthermore negotiate very successfully with the Croats in the way that was crowned in 1925 with the establishment of the coalition government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Are you acquainted with the research of Ivo Banac?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banac, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Question in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you agree with his assessment of activity of Nikola Pasic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Ivo Banac gives more weight to Pasic's influence within the Serbian political establishment at the end of World War I than is warranted by history because had Regent Aleksandar followed Pasic's advice, the constitutional arrangement on which the kingdom was based would look very different. Quite possibly, it would have sought a more clearcut definition of Serbian unit within the new kingdom. But really, while I'm familiar with Ivo Banac's work and I respect him, I do not recall specific judgement of Pasic's role that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher, please, to distribute the excerpts of this book to the parties, and one for the registry. And please give us the next J exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: J32, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: Dr. Trifkovic, would you agree that political and state system of Yugoslavia as established after the Second World War was so destructive by its very nature?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Is it true that after the collapse of the communist regime in the former Yugoslavia, the Serb political leadership made an attempt to preserve state unity and prevent the disintegration of Yugoslavia? And when this attempt failed, opted for the implementation of a Greater Serbia concept in order to create ethnically-homogeneous Serb state on the Serbian historical lands?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with the first part of your assessment, Your Honour, about the attempt to keep Yugoslavia together. As for the concerted effort to follow the greater Serbian plan, I would doubt very much this was indeed the Milosevic scenario or the only scenario. I have reason to believe that Milosevic played several games, so to say, and that even some of his closest collaborators were not quite certain what was the ultimate end game even if he had one. It is a very complex issue and I regret that I cannot give a more clearcut answer, but it is the one that I sincerely hold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the last question: Isn't it true that trying to prevent the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia and to implement a Greater Serbia concept, the Serbian political leadership recoursed to the use of armed force accompanied by flagrant violations of international humanitarian law and generally recognised standards of human rights?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that on the Serbian side, there had been recourse to force and the violation of all these rights that you mention. It is also true that the way in which the separation was being effected, particularly in the case of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, violated Yugoslav constitutional norms, and created the sense of insecurity and uncertainty among the very sizable Serbian population of those republics. To simply state that one side resorted to violence without considering the complexity of the multilayered and multicornered equation is too simplistic. I believe that part of the problem we have had ever since the beginning of Yugoslavia's disintegration is the attempt to look at things through the prism of black and white. Most of the Yugoslav story is mainly different shadows of grey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Trifkovic. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Only one. I hope it's only one question, Dr. Trifkovic. Are you aware that the Islamic declaration by Mr. Izetbegovic was published in 1970?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The publication in 1970 had the semi-illicit character. The formal and, how shall I put it, mainstream trumpeted publication only came under the Bosna edition in 1990. But, of course, yes, the text had been available since 1970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Why do you call it semi-illicit character?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because under the rule of the old socialist Yugoslavia, for a publication to have the licit character, you have to have "retzin zenti," [phoen] which means two reviewers who recommend a piece of work for the publication and who invest their professional reputation and their standing behind the given work. And this is something that takes me quite a few years back. I wouldn't like to give you a more detailed answer than this. Suffice to say that under the 1970 publication, the procedural rules for the legal distribution and dissemination of the book with the national library entry card were not satisfied. But at the same time, as far as I'm aware, the 1990 edition was not qualitatively different from the preliminary 1970 write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: As long as I can see, they are identical?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So can you tell me why after 20 years, you decided, or a lot of people decided, that this is an revelation of an extremist character when in the Islamic declaration, Bosnia is not even mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't need to mention Bosnia in order to display through the statements such as we are all familiar with, that you have very strong views of the desirable organisation of the society along the lines of a clerically-ordained and clearly religiously-inspired preferred order of human affairs. In fact, I don't think that it would have been even necessary to refer to any particular geographic region, even though he does refer to the entire Islamic world from Morocco to South East Asia to Indonesia. The blueprint is there, the principle is there, and its implications for the non-Muslim communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina could not have been comforting, quite the contrary, I believe they are rightfully alarming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Only one more question then relating to this: If you replace Islamic by Christian or Jewish declaration, wouldn't it be a lyrical declaration of what a person could think about an ideal society?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question is very interesting because right now the only attempt to contextualise Christianity with the social and political order comes from certain marginal Protestant groups in the deep south Bible belt of the United States, a sustained Catholic integralism or orthodox fundamentalism that seeks to recreate, for instance, Byzantine of the 6th century AD or the papal states of medieval times simply does not exist as a viable political project anywhere in the world. At the same time, political Islam does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes to 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. When the expert is in the courtroom again, it's for the Defence. And please don't forget that at the end, we have to decide whether you want to tender or not. But please proceed. Further examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, good afternoon, Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to be pretty fast to conclude in the next half an hour, so -- to enable you to leave tonight. Can you tell us, what's the title of your column in Chronicles magazine?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the print variety, there is "The American Interest." Would you like a specimen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, just tell us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the Internet variety, "News and Views Unfit to Print".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "News and Views Unfit to Print"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that you are prone to criticise and that's actually your job to criticise [Realtime transcript read in error "credit advertise"]?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also the Internet column is more polemical, more -- how shall I put. Generally, Internet equivalence of print publications are less stringently edited and less rigorously subjected to the checks and balances which apply in print journalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 117, line 12, it says "credit advertise," it should say "criticise." You criticised also this Tribunal at least in 1996. Are you aware that this Tribunal has been criticised also by some of the Judges of the Tribunal? And we would like to distribute, to distribute some documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is an agreed fact, and it has nothing to do, I think -- yes, it's an ongoing procedure, let us put this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition, let me reiterate what I already stated yesterday, that first of all my 1996 article is the one that was the basis for the consideration of this subject yesterday, and that after the passage of seven years, my personal hope that I had entertained at that time, that domestic judicial systems of the success of republics would be better equipped to deal with the task themselves has failed to be fully materialised. And at the same time, this Tribunal has become more even-handed in the treatment of indictments and at least potential culpability of different sides which would have made me express opinions on this subject in a more considered way today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree with me that criticism can be constructive as well?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criticism indeed has to exist in order for the dialectical process of the enrichment of human knowledge and experience to proceed, if the hegelian parallel is allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also criticised former president of Yugoslavia Milosevic, and you stated it, and I have a list of some of your titles. I'll just ask you whether you remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it would help if I explained that these articles were put to him not for whether he's justified in criticising. I said he was. But for the basis of the allegations that he made, not for anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we quote some -- a few titles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have the statement as such. We have, in addition, the summary of articles, radio interviews, and so on and so forth. If it would be in addition to this, yes; if not, then we have the statement before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just quote three or four so Your Honours have a rough idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From US News and World Report, June 18th, 1990, it says: "Slobodan Milosevic is cynically exploiting the nationalist awakening to perpetrator communist rule and his own power in the eastern half of Yugoslavia." And it's addressed as your text. Is it true, Dr. Trifkovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. And it -- this statement relates to a question from the panel a minute ago about Milosevic's motivation, which as I tried to explain, is multilayered, and it is very hard to tell which was the real Milosevic, especially at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And standard, Hoover Institution in 1991, published under the title "The Yugoslav Crisis and the United States" that you called Mr. Milosevic "demagogue and populist"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used that phrase more than one, and I believe that this was one of those occasions. "Populist and demagogue" is I think a very apt term throughout his misrule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the "Plain Dealer," Cleveland, September 6th, 1992, they quoted you and said: "Trifkovic said he was critical of the authoritarian rule of Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic and has called for his removal from office and democratic reforms." Do you remember that you were quoted by this paper?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes. Yes, I believe that is an accurate quote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And out of 20 others, I would like to choose that you in the Times, London, on November 23rd, 1995, you said, and I quote: "Trusting Milosevic is like giving a blank bloodbank to Count Dracula."

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an article by Ivan Prentice [phoen] quoting me as far as I remember, and yes, it is an accurate quote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would just add another one where you say: "Milosevic is afraid of having Mladic and Karadzic delivered to The Hague not because of the possibility of a Serb backlash in Serbia itself but because those two know quite a lot about Milosevic's own rule in the early days of the Yugoslavian war in 1991 and 1992." It's BBC source, World Service TV, 29th of May, 1996.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an accurate quote, too, I think. Yes, sounds right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to show you the document marked in this trial as S16, SK46. It's from Donia collection. So Doctor, in front of you, you have the B/C/S version if I can see correctly.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can please turn page 2, and because it's B/C/S, I'll read in B/C/S as we both know that you can follow. In the middle of the page, there is the name of Stakic, Milomir. Or if you can use the English version, if it's easier for you. Do you find name Stakic, Milomir?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read it. "Stakic, Milomir, [Interpretation] since 30 April 1992, here in the Municipality of Prijedor the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been implemented. Along with those laws which conform with the constitution. In those matters where new laws have not been passed, the existent laws are still applied. The next two or three months until the funds which are now being established actually have available fund will be the most critical period. Peace must be maintained at all costs, and the economy must be revived." [In English] You were asked by the Prosecution that Dr. Stakic gave a statement in September, October 1992 when all the Muslims have already been removed from the municipality. From which date is this record or minutes, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9th of May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, what was, if you know, the situation regarding the national structure of the population in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The straightforward answer is difficult because some people had started leaving spontaneously in the period even while the multiethnic Municipal Assembly was still functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But maybe I can ask you this way: Was the period immediately after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your question, the drastic departure of the bulk of people who had left by October of 1992 had not left to the best of my knowledge at the time when this report was prepared, i.e., the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember reading these minutes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I remember seeing reference to the statement about the need for the observance of laws in the Kozarski Vjesnik. What I do not specifically remember is in that article, the mention of the validity of the inherited old legislation, but it would stand to reason that, of course, unless new legislation is enacted, then the inherited one would remain on the statute books.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we won't be needing that document any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony, on page 54, line 14 today, you mentioned, and you were shown the document with the name of Mate Boban. Which political party Mr. Mate Boban was a member and which function he carried in the spring and summer 1992, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban belonged to the Croatian democratic union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in the spring of 1992, as its leader, he was representative of the Croatian -- I think it could be accurately said Croatian people because the HDZ -- HDZ, for all intents and purposes, was the political force that represented most Croats in the Cutileiro-related negotiations that were underway in Sarajevo, Lisbon, Grac, and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this document, which number is bears, with the entitle "Through Bosnian Eyes" by Robert Donia -- no, actually by Mirko Pejanovic, introductory remarks by Robert Donia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mirko Pejanovic wrote a booklet or -- I don't know, we have only a few pages, with the title "Through Bosnian Eyes" and you were asked about him being a member of a -- some political structures as a representative of Serbian people. You answered that he was never elected by Serbs in Bosnia. And this gentleman actually commented on unconstitutional act in defiance of parliament's authority. What is the profession of Mr. Mirko Pejanovic if you know?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what is the profession of Mirko Pejanovic, and I would be very surprised if it was law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not, but I cannot testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't put it in, but I've got the full book here, and there's a biography of what he did so I'll have that copied and it will be handed in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, is it the same name on the first page, on the bottom of the page -- actually in the introductory page, that says that introduction and notes "by Robert J. Donia"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the same name appear on an expert statement of a historian, expert historian offered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear to be so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can confirm it is, but I would like to know what the suggestion is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please don't have unnecessary disputes. The Trial Chamber is able to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to rush through the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked today about the factual basis for a plea of guilty of Ms. Plavsic. And wasn't it obvious from this document that this document is not composed by Ms. Plavsic, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object. I haven't objected to any of the leading questions so far. It is not a proper question to put, as far as anyone knows, that is Mrs. Plavsic's basis of plea. You cannot ask a question like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rephrase. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 10, it says: "By October 1991, the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Ms. Plavsic..." Does this paragraph show that somebody else composed this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object. It's a leading question. Do you understand what a leading question is, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may ask the witness for his opinion if you really want to, but in nonleading form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, stay polite vis-a-vis each other. But I think the objection is well-based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it common, Mr. Trifkovic, in our language or in English that somebody composes a document mentioning himself in a third person singular?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is for royalty and patriarchs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It is not common that anybody else uses and describes him or herself in a singular third?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really feel unable to comment on Mrs. Plavsic's role in preparing her own statement. I really prefer to stick to responses that I gave to the prosecutorial team, and give her the deserved respect of the benefit of the doubt in this respect. But at least emphasise the possibility that the sentiments and opinions expressed in the statement are by themselves not the final establishment of the existence of the agreed set of guidelines and the agreed set of objectives common to the entire SDS leadership. I really don't feel qualified to comment on the personal circumstances of the preparation of her statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Regarding the plebiscite, you explained us that it's not binding for anybody, but it's only the expression of one nation. What is the reason that there were two coloured papers or ballot papers at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that people not declaring themselves as Serbs could also join in the voting, which by the way all together was a silly and not particularly useful form of -- it's one of the examples of ad hoc improvisations that were both politically and substantively ill-conceived. By describing what it was, I'm not suggesting that it was a very fortuitous way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Trifkovic. We want to be sure that you will leave on time, and we don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Questions in return? This is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I should make it very clear because Dr. Trifkovic said he had to leave today, there were a number of other aspects, factual assertions in his report, that I was unable to cover. I want to make it absolutely clear that the Prosecution suggests that this report in many other respects than those we have covered is factually inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's a good time to prepare the oral submissions and the final brief, and this is the place to discuss also this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the trouble. I haven't actually put to him the documents that I would have put otherwise. But, Your Honour, I just wanted to make that clear that should it be -- should the Defence be going to assert that other parts of his report were not challenged by me, in many cases that is because we didn't have sufficient time. I just want to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If this is a mutual agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that sometimes we were rushed as well with some Prosecution witnesses. If it's applied to anybody, we would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I had the impression that you also deleted a number of documents and therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we skipped many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's only fair to give both parties the rights to address this statement as such, and the testimony as reflected on the transcript, and none of the parties - that's my understanding - will object on the mere basis that the one or other document was not put to this witness. Can we agree on this? Thank you. Then the first question is of course: Is it the intention of the Defence to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic mentioned only chapter 5, if I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not my intention to treat the entire book as a document, but because I was specifically asked about the role of mujahedin in Bosnia during the early 1990s and couldn't quote details from memory, I wanted simply the relevant segment of the book to be treated as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we would like to offer Chapter 5 from this book in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, here we -- it's really a borderline question about the relevance for our concrete case. We have the comments in the transcript by the witness, and I really can't see in the moment the added probative value of this. I want to refrain from characterising this paper. So can we agree that it's not relevant for the purpose of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask the usher, please, to give these books back to the witness. And also, Madam Registrar, your copy, and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd rather like to keep it because in fact it's wholly unavailable in this country. And although we had quotes from it, you never know, it may be useful to keep. So I would like to keep it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for it to be made an exhibit, but I would simply like to hold on to the copy, as it was volunteered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was volunteered in the context of a document that could be potentially accepted by the Court as part of the official record. It was simply not volunteered as my personal gift to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Trifkovic, that book will be returned to you, and we'll see if we can get hold of a copy somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So also this issue has been clarified. We have a number of documents not yet admitted, but we have to do it in the presence of the expert in case there should be any kind of dispute. Now, in the order backwards, first, it was S424, Security Assessment for the Prijedor Municipality. Objections? 424, Security Assessment for the Prijedor Municipality, 23 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object. It's outside of the scope of the indictment, and I think that that document, I cannot find it, is not signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Prosecution, please. May I hear the submission by the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the objection. Your Honour, we have been through this a number of times. It was written after the period of the indictment; however, it refers fairly and squarely to all the events within the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In fact, we have to base our decision not on the date when it was written, but it's related to the period starting May 1992. Therefore, it's in the scope, and therefore admitted into evidence, S424A and B respectively. S423. These are the proposals or opinions by Mr. Badinter. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S423A and B respectively. S422. Unfortunately, we don't have the cover page, but I can identify it in Cyrillic, the minutes and tape recording of the national assembly's 17th session held on 24-26 July 1992. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not have objections, although we would like to have these kind of documents if possible, because this one has never been disclosed to us before. And if the Prosecution has a similar document, we think that it would be necessary for us to have them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If there are additional problems between the parties, please resolve this problem amongst yourselves. In the moment, we have only this document before us. Admitted into evidence, S422A and B respectively. S421, document of 6 March 1992, signed by President Mirko Boskovic. Objections?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The announcement of the results of the referendum.
